title: A protected default-branch checkout is not a safe workspace
summary: Hooks and branch protections can block commits, pushes, merges, or ref updates while still allowing ordinary file edits. Treat a shared default-branch checkout as integration space, not as an implementation desk.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid contaminating shared checkouts with unattributed dirty files that later sessions may accidentally adopt, clean, or publish.

contexts: a repository has a shared default-branch checkout plus separate feature branches, worktrees, worklanes, or desks for implementation
commit or push hooks protect the default checkout but editors, generators, and formatters can still write files
a later agent is asked to clean, reuse, or reason about a dirty default checkout

trigger_signals.description: The default checkout shows modified, staged, or untracked files from unrelated work.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Stop treating the checkout as a safe desk; classify and preserve residue before cleanup.

trigger_signals.description: A hook or branch protection blocks commit, merge, rebase, push, or ref update from the default checkout.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Remember that landing protection does not prevent ordinary file mutation.

trigger_signals.description: Plain `git diff` is empty but status still reports staged changes.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Inspect the index with cached diff or porcelain status before declaring the checkout clean.

negative_signals.description: The repository is intentionally single-user and uses the default checkout as its only workspace.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Ordinary branch hygiene may be enough when there is no shared integration checkout.

negative_signals.description: The task is read-only and no command can write caches, generated artifacts, or formatter output.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A read-only inspection does not create the workspace-contamination failure mode.

common_wrong_assumptions: If hooks prevent commit or push, editing the protected checkout is safe.
A clean `git diff` proves there is no local residue.
A future agent can infer ownership of dirty files from filenames alone.

first_checks.check: Before editing, verify the intended path is not the shared default checkout.
first_checks.why: This prevents implementation work from starting in the integration surface.

first_checks.check: Check both worktree and index state in the default checkout.
first_checks.why: Staged-only residue can hide from plain diff output.

first_checks.check: If the default checkout is dirty, preserve a status/diff summary before cleanup.
first_checks.why: Unknown work is evidence before it is clutter.

decision_rules.condition: The default checkout is dirty before a new implementation task starts.
decision_rules.then: Do not implement there. Capture evidence, classify ownership, and move the new task to the intended feature branch, worktree, or lane.

decision_rules.condition: A hook blocks landing from the default checkout but file edits are possible.
decision_rules.then: Keep landing hooks, but add an edit-time or session-start guard that fails early when the shared default checkout is dirty.

do_not: Do not rely on commit or push hooks to prevent uncommitted edits.
Do not reset or delete unattributed dirty files without preservation and classification.
Do not mix unrelated default-checkout residue into the current task.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Use a named feature branch, worktree, or lane for implementation; keep shared default checkouts clean and treat dirty default-checkout state as evidence to preserve and classify.

risk.notes: This record concerns workflow hygiene. It does not authorize destructive cleanup of unknown edits or changing repository protections.

sources.supports: Final six-candidate review found the preventive default-checkout workspace trap public-worthy, with dissent that it could merge into orphan-work cleanup.
sources.excerpt: Protected default-branch hooks do not make the default checkout a safe workspace.

title: Degraded semantic search is not evidence that a rule or spec is absent
summary: When a retrieval, vector, or semantic search reports degradation - embedding-generation failure, an unbuilt or stale approximate index, a fallback to keyword-only, a shard failure, a timeout, or partial results - an agent must not treat an empty or irrelevant result as proof that a rule, spec, doc, or prior decision does not exist. Empty-under-degradation is a recall artifact, not verified absence. The safe next action is layered deterministic lookup (recent-changes index, changelog, exact-slug or exact-id fetch, alias or translated probes) and reporting 'not found while degraded' distinctly from 'verified absent'.
ai_value: Prevents agents from implementing from memory, re-deriving an existing policy, or violating a durable rule because retrieval was silently degraded. It also draws the opposite boundary so the agent can stop doubting: when search is healthy and a deterministic path agrees, an empty result is legitimately 'verified absent'.

contexts: an agent queries a vector, semantic, or RAG knowledge base or doc portal to find operating rules, specs, runbooks, or prior decisions before acting

the retrieval layer can degrade independently of the underlying data (embedding-generation failure, unbuilt or stale approximate index, fallback to keyword-only, shard failure, query timeout, or partial results)
the search response can carry an in-band health or partiality signal (a warning flag, a timed_out field, shard-failure counts, or a fallback/partial/degraded marker)

a deterministic lookup path exists alongside semantic search: an exact-slug or exact-id fetch from an authoritative store, an append-only recent-changes or changelog index, a table of contents, or a file listing

trigger_signals.description: The search response carries any in-band degradation or partiality signal. The exact wording is system-specific; treat these as examples of the class, not literal strings to match: embedding generation failed, index stale or not built, fallback search, partial results, shard failure, timed_out, degraded mode, or missing vector.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Recall is impaired. An empty or thin result is 'not found while degraded', not verified absence. Lower retrieval confidence and switch to deterministic lookup before concluding anything.

trigger_signals.description: A natural-language semantic query returns nothing for a topic that very likely has durable rules or prior decisions, with no degradation flag present. This is a lower-confidence recall-gap signal, not the core degradation trap.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat as a recall-gap hypothesis to test with one deterministic probe, not as proof of absence. Do not escalate indefinitely.

trigger_signals.description: The human or handoff uses domain language, feature names, or a non-English alias that differs from stored slugs, titles, or aliases.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: A miss may be vocabulary or language mismatch rather than absence. Re-probe with translated keywords, aliases, and known identifiers.

trigger_signals.description: A recently mentioned new rule or operating-surface change cannot be found by semantic search.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Fresh content may not be embedded or indexed yet. Check the append-only recent-changes or changelog path directly.

negative_signals.description: The search self-reports healthy and complete retrieval (no degradation, partiality, or fallback flag; timed_out is false; shards all successful) AND a deterministic path (exact-id, index, changelog, table of contents, or file listing) also returns nothing.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Two independent paths agreeing on absence is real evidence of absence. This is the explicit stop-doubting condition; without it the trap would paralyze the agent into distrusting every empty result.

negative_signals.description: An exact-identifier lookup (known slug, id, or filename) against the authoritative store returns a definitive not-found (a 404, not a timeout or error).
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A deterministic point lookup that authoritatively says the id does not exist is verified absence even when the semantic layer is degraded; degradation impairs ranking and recall, not exact-key existence.

negative_signals.description: The agent has no prior reason to expect a durable rule, spec, or decision for this query (no handoff mention, no domain convention, a novel one-off topic).
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Absence of evidence is only suspicious when the prior probability of a record is non-trivial; otherwise empty is the expected answer and re-probing wastes effort.

negative_signals.description: The degradation flag is for a subsystem unrelated to the lookup actually performed (for example a reranker warning while the keyword index used is healthy).
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Prevents treating any warning anywhere in the response as poisoning an otherwise sound deterministic result, which would re-introduce paralysis.

common_wrong_assumptions: The search returned no hit, so the rule or spec probably does not exist.
If semantic search cannot find it, it is safe to proceed from memory.
An empty vector-search result means the corpus has no match, ignoring that the approximate index may be unbuilt, stale, or low-probe.
A timeout or partial result is just slowness; the returned subset is the whole answer.
Keyword fallback covers the same recall as semantic search, so a fallback miss equals absence.

first_checks.check: Inspect the search response for degradation: warning flags, timed_out, shard failures, fallback/partial/degraded markers; record whether retrieval was semantic, keyword-only, or degraded.
first_checks.why: Real engines signal degradation in-band; reading it converts an ambiguous empty result into a known degraded state.

first_checks.check: Query the append-only recent-changes index, decision index, changelog, table of contents, or file list directly.
first_checks.why: Deterministic enumeration does not depend on similarity ranking or approximate-index recall, so it can confirm presence the embedding path missed.

first_checks.check: Re-probe with concrete slug fragments, translated keywords, aliases, feature names, and known identifiers from the handoff or task brief.
first_checks.why: Many misses are vocabulary or language mismatches rather than absence.

first_checks.check: Do an exact-id or exact-slug point fetch against the authoritative store.
first_checks.why: A definitive 404 confirms absence; a timeout or error confirms the lookup itself is still degraded.

first_checks.check: If recall still looks broken, label the result 'not found under degraded search' and continue only the reversible part of the task or stop, rather than silently changing behavior.
first_checks.why: Preserves the absence-versus-degraded distinction for the current report and for future agents without unbounded escalation.

decision_rules.condition: The search response shows a degradation signal (embedding failure, stale/unbuilt index, fallback, partial results, shard failure, or timed_out) and the result is empty or irrelevant.
decision_rules.then: Do not conclude absence. Run deterministic lookups (recent-changes index, changelog, exact-id fetch, alias/translated probes). Only after a healthy path agrees may you reason about absence.

decision_rules.condition: A durable rule or spec may exist but retrieval is degraded and unconfirmed, and the next action depends on that rule.
decision_rules.then: Hold the dependent implementation; keep the next action reversible or stop and record a single bounded diagnostic follow-up.

decision_rules.condition: Search is healthy (no degradation flags) AND a deterministic path (exact-id 404 or exhaustive bounded index read) both report the item absent.
decision_rules.then: Record 'verified absent' with the two confirming paths and proceed normally; this trap does not apply.

decision_rules.condition: A healthy search returns empty with no degradation flag, but you have prior reason to expect a record exists.
decision_rules.then: Run one deterministic probe (exact-id or recent-changes index). If it also returns nothing, accept absence; do not loop indefinitely. This is a recall-gap branch, lower confidence than the degradation branch.

decision_rules.condition: The final report will state that a rule, spec, or doc was not found.
decision_rules.then: Explicitly tag which it is and name the paths checked, so downstream agents inherit the correct retrieval confidence.

do_not: Do not infer nonexistence from an empty semantic result when the tool reported embedding, index, timeout, or partial-result warnings.
Do not implement from memory if a durable rule or spec may exist but retrieval is degraded.
Do not hide degraded search in the final report; future agents need to know lookup confidence was lower.
Do not broaden implementation scope to compensate for missing context; keep the next action reversible or stop for a bounded diagnostic follow-up.
Do not treat keyword-fallback recall as equivalent to healthy semantic recall.
Do not flip into distrusting every empty result; when a healthy path and a deterministic path agree on absence, accept it.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Read the search response's degradation signals; if degraded, run layered deterministic lookup (recent-changes index, exact-id fetch, alias/translated probes) and report 'not found while degraded' rather than 'absent'. Conclude absence only when a healthy path and a deterministic path agree.

risk.notes: The trap's safe action is additional read-only lookup and honest reporting, which is low direct risk. Risk becomes high only indirectly when the missed rule governs a hard gate (security, auth, billing, permissions, deploy, or destructive operations); in that case the downstream action carries the gate, not this lookup. This record authorizes extra read-only lookup and accurate reporting only.

sources.excerpt: If true and there are shard request timeouts or shard failures, the request returns partial results. ... If false, it returns an error with no partial results. ... [timeout] The period of time to wait for a response from each shard. If no response is received before the timeout expires, the request fails and returns an error.
sources.supports: Official proof that a healthy-looking search can return partial (incomplete) results on shard timeout or failure, and that this is surfaced in-band. Establishes that an empty or partial result set is not the complete corpus answer.

sources.excerpt: Unlike typical indexes, you will see different results for queries after adding an approximate index. ... Create the index after the table has some data. ... [ivfflat.probes] A higher value provides better recall at the cost of speed.
sources.supports: Official proof that an approximate vector index legitimately returns different or incomplete results depending on whether the index is built and on probe settings, so 'no vector hit' can be an index-state artifact rather than corpus absence.

sources.excerpt: Altman DG, Bland JM. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. BMJ. 1995 Aug 19;311(7003):485. A non-significant or null result does not demonstrate that no effect or difference exists; it indicates insufficient evidence to detect one.
sources.supports: Neutral, citable grounding for the core epistemic claim: a low-power or degraded probe yields absence of evidence, which must not be reported as evidence of absence.

sources.excerpt: Offline deterministic reproducer over a tiny neutral corpus: three degraded modes (embedding_failed, index_not_built, timeout_partial) each return an empty semantic result with a degradation flag while an exact-id lookup still returns the document; a healthy search plus an authoritative exact-id 404 returns verified_absent; a healthy miss on an existing doc returns recall_gap_not_absent.
sources.supports: Public-safe demonstration that empty-under-degradation is not absence, and that the stop-doubting boundary (healthy plus deterministic agreement) yields a legitimate verified-absent verdict.

environment.os_context: local Linux session, no network, no private data

verification_runs.observed_result: All six checks PASS: the three degraded modes each return verdict=not_found_while_degraded with an empty hit set, a degradation flag set, and a successful exact-id lookup; healthy present-doc returns found; healthy plus exact-id 404 returns verified_absent; healthy miss on an existing doc returns recall_gap_not_absent. RESULT: ALL PASS (exit 0).
verification_runs.conclusion: Empty-under-degradation is distinguishable from true absence by an exact-id cross-check, and the verified-absent boundary holds, so an agent can both avoid false-absence conclusions and avoid distrusting every empty result.

title: Exercise new guardrails on the patch that introduces them
summary: A process rule is weakest at the moment it is added. Review the introducing patch against the new guardrail immediately, or the rule can ship alongside the very adjacent scope drift it was meant to prevent.
ai_value: Helps agents turn process changes into practiced behavior by catching unrelated behavior, UI, data-shape, or rule changes inside the first patch that claims to forbid them.

contexts: a patch adds or amends a guardrail, policy, hook, wrapper check, or review rule
the same patch also contains nearby convenience changes
success state is narrow enough that adjacent improvements can be separated

trigger_signals.description: The patch changes a rule and also changes unrelated behavior names, UI/data shape, default values, or workflow semantics.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Compare every behavior change against the declared success state, including the new rule itself.

trigger_signals.description: Review language praises the new guardrail but does not test whether this patch obeys it.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Ask for a concrete pass/fail disposition for out-of-scope changes.

negative_signals.description: The extra change is required to make the guardrail enforceable or to keep existing behavior working.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: It may be in scope, but the rationale should be stated explicitly.

negative_signals.description: The patch only changes wording and no behavior, rule semantics, data shape, or operation surface.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A lighter review may be enough.

common_wrong_assumptions: A new guardrail is valuable even if the introducing patch violates it.
Adjacent cleanup is harmless when it is near the rule being edited.
Reviewing for the new rule can wait until the next patch.

first_checks.check: List the declared success state and every behavior/rule/data-shape change in the patch.
first_checks.why: This makes adjacent scope drift visible instead of relying on reviewer memory.

first_checks.check: Ask an independent reviewer to name any out-of-scope adjacent change and its disposition.
first_checks.why: The reviewer should explicitly say removed, deferred, or intentionally re-scoped.

first_checks.check: Move unrelated improvements into residual notes or follow-up candidates.
first_checks.why: The first use of the guardrail should model the behavior future agents must follow.

decision_rules.condition: The introducing patch contains an improvement not needed for the declared success state.
decision_rules.then: Remove it from the patch or explicitly re-scope with review evidence before merging.

decision_rules.condition: A nearby change is necessary for enforcement or compatibility.
decision_rules.then: Keep it only with a written rationale tying it to the success state.

do_not: Do not use a guardrail patch as cover for unrelated behavior changes.
Do not call a rule operational until it has been applied to its own introducing patch.
Do not leave the disposition of adjacent improvements only in chat.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Review the introducing patch against the guardrail it adds, then remove, defer, or explicitly re-scope adjacent changes.

risk.notes: Mostly process hygiene; risk rises if the guardrail affects security, permissions, publication, or deployment gates.

sources.excerpt: The first patch containing a new guardrail should be reviewed against that guardrail so unrelated adjacent changes are removed, deferred, or explicitly re-scoped.
sources.supports: Provides a de-identified internal closeout seed with failure condition, early signs, avoidance, and verification method; Claude and Gemini deliberation on 2026-06-01 judged it public-worthy.

title: Request-side datetime filters need literal and precision checks
summary: A differential import can repeatedly fetch the same records when an external search API accepts a timestamp filter string but silently honors only the date portion or a lower precision than the cursor uses.
ai_value: Helps agents debug cursor-advances-but-membership-does-not-change symptoms at the upstream query-parser boundary instead of chasing downstream deduplication first.

contexts: scheduled imports or differential syncs use text-based external API search syntax
a saved cursor timestamp moves forward
query strings include datetime literals, quotes, offsets, or fractional seconds

trigger_signals.description: Each run returns the same small count and the same record identities even though the saved cursor advances.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Check result membership against the cursor before blaming upsert deduplication.

trigger_signals.description: Upsert metrics are mostly or entirely unchanged, such as saved count equaling unchanged count.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: This can be an upstream filter-literal issue, not only a downstream no-op.

trigger_signals.description: The external API accepts the raw query without a clear parse error.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Accepted syntax is not proof that the intended precision was honored.

trigger_signals.description: Boundary-count checks around the exact cursor time do not explain the repeated membership.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The parser may be truncating or rounding before comparison.

negative_signals.description: Another ingestion path legitimately saved the same records first.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Repeated unchanged rows can be a valid race with another writer; compare record identities and write timing.

negative_signals.description: Multiple notifications point to the same entity by design.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Repeated entity IDs may reflect provider event semantics rather than parser precision.

negative_signals.description: The external API documentation explicitly supports the exact quote, offset, and fractional precision being sent and a fixture proves membership changes.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then inspect downstream deduplication or cursor storage next.

common_wrong_assumptions: A moving cursor means the upstream query is narrowing the result set.
If the API did not reject the query, it understood every timestamp character as intended.
Unchanged upserts always mean downstream deduplication is working correctly.

first_checks.check: Log or snapshot the final query string in a redacted safe form.
first_checks.why: Agents need the literal actually sent, not just the intended cursor value.

first_checks.check: Assert the provider-documented quote, offset, and timestamp precision in a query-builder test.
first_checks.why: External search syntax is a parser contract.

first_checks.check: Verify with real or fixture data that changing the cursor changes result membership, not only aggregate counts.
first_checks.why: Membership is the discriminator for truncation/rounding.

first_checks.check: Compare this request/query-side literal issue with any response-side timezone or nested-model record before merging hypotheses.
first_checks.why: The related public record covers different API shape failures.

decision_rules.condition: Cursor advances but returned identities remain fixed and the outbound datetime literal does not match documented quote/precision form.
decision_rules.then: Change the query builder to emit the documented literal form, including quotes and supported precision, then rerun a membership-changing fixture.

decision_rules.condition: Repeated unchanged rows are explained by another writer, duplicate notifications, or a stable dataset boundary.
decision_rules.then: Do not apply the parser-precision trap; investigate the real repeated-write mechanism.

do_not: Do not expand production import scope to test the hypothesis.
Do not log raw credentials or private customer identifiers in query evidence.
Do not merge this with response-side timezone or nested-model failures without preserving the request-side membership discriminator.

Do not include private service names, internal URLs, account identifiers, incident identifiers, private repository paths, tenant/store names, setup-card field names, low-level endpoint strings or organization-specific tooling in public lessons.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Capture the exact safe query string, match documented datetime literal precision, and prove cursor changes alter result membership.

risk.notes: This public record is de-identified and does not authorize live mutation, publication, credential, permission, billing, data, or availability changes by itself.

sources.supports: Original de-identified request/query-side datetime filter candidate; synthesis required a cross-reference to the existing response-side external API record.
Claude and Gemini independent deliberations plus curator synthesis selected this de-identified record for publication and specified required narrowing, splitting, cross-links, and hold boundaries.

title: External contracts need authoritative observation, not inference
summary: When automating an external UI, one-shot protocol, or partner API, do not infer the contract from memory, public hints, or adjacent examples. Collect live, official, authorized evidence before implementation or enablement.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid hallucinated selectors, burned bootstrap tokens, and guessed authenticated fields by insisting on the right evidence source for each external contract.

contexts: browser automation against a third-party single-page UI
one-shot bootstrap or exchange protocols with credentials or session tokens
partner, authenticated, or sandbox-only API fields not fully described in public docs

trigger_signals.description: The agent is writing selectors for a UI it does not own without a fresh page artifact.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Pause implementation and capture a read-only live UI artifact first.

trigger_signals.description: A one-shot credential or bootstrap token must be exchanged exactly once.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Use tested helper code or explicit protocol docs; do not reconstruct the request shape from a short card.

trigger_signals.description: Required mapper fields are missing from public docs but seem guessable from examples.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Block enablement until authorized docs or sandbox evidence confirms the fields.

negative_signals.description: The target contract is owned by the project and covered by current tests or source.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Use the project source and tests; external-contract recon may not be needed.

negative_signals.description: The work is read-only documentation triage that will not call the external system or enable behavior.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Record uncertainty clearly rather than implementing from it.

common_wrong_assumptions: A prior memory of the UI is good enough for selectors.
Public examples reveal authenticated partner fields.
A plausible token exchange shape is safe to try because the credential can be retried.

first_checks.check: Identify the authoritative evidence source for the contract.
first_checks.why: DOM needs live observation; protocols need exact helper/tests; authenticated APIs need official or sandbox evidence.

first_checks.check: Capture or cite the evidence before implementation or enablement.
first_checks.why: The implementation should point to observed selectors, exact protocol fields, or confirmed mapper fields.

first_checks.check: Add tests for the confirmed contract shape and failure modes.
first_checks.why: Tests prevent later agents from re-inventing the same external contract.

decision_rules.condition: A contract is external and volatile or credential-sensitive.
decision_rules.then: Stop guessing; collect the appropriate live, official, authorized, or tested evidence before writing or enabling code.

decision_rules.condition: The first attempt consumed or may consume a one-shot credential.
decision_rules.then: Do not retry with guessed shapes; preserve redacted evidence and route through the approved credential recovery path.

do_not: Do not write third-party SPA selectors from memory.
Do not spend one-shot credentials to test plausible request shapes.
Do not fill authenticated API fields from public examples unless authorized evidence confirms them.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Name the external contract, gather the right authoritative observation for that contract, and only then implement or enable behavior.

risk.notes: This public record is de-identified. It does not authorize bypassing human, maintainer, security, publication, billing, data, or credential gates.

sources.excerpt: Browser automation against a third-party SPA failed repeatedly when selectors were guessed instead of observed from a live read-only page artifact.
sources.supports: Supports the live-recon mechanism.

sources.excerpt: A general agent can infer a plausible but wrong one-shot bootstrap exchange and consume the only credential before storing the returned session correctly.
sources.supports: Supports helper-first, tested one-shot protocol handling.

sources.excerpt: Authenticated provider mapper fields may be absent from public docs; guessing required fields risks incorrect enablement.
sources.supports: Supports authorized-docs or sandbox-evidence requirements.

title: GitHub Actions cost skips need a safety boundary
summary: When optimizing GitHub Actions spend, agents may add path filters, job-level conditions, broad concurrency cancellation, or tighter timeouts without checking whether the skipped work is a required status check, a safety guard, or a source/config boundary check. The safe first move is to separate cost evidence from safety semantics before editing workflows.
ai_value: Helps coding and operations agents reduce CI spend without making required checks disappear, inverting label/scope guards, missing config-triggered boundary risks, or setting timeouts from intuition instead of run-duration evidence.

contexts: an agent is asked to reduce GitHub Actions spend, runner minutes, workflow frequency, or CI cost
a proposed workflow edit adds or tightens paths, paths-ignore, branches, job-level if conditions, concurrency.cancel-in-progress, or timeout-minutes
a repository has required status checks, branch protection, rulesets, safety guard workflows, import-boundary checks, or release/deploy-adjacent CI
a workflow appears cheap per run but runs on many pull requests or push events
a safety guard normally exits early because the changed files, labels, or PR scope do not require deeper validation

tools.name: GitHub Actions
tools.version_range: current public GitHub Actions semantics as of 2026-05-10

trigger_signals.description: The task mentions high Actions spend, runner minutes, budget exhaustion, docs-only skips, reducing workflow frequency, or cheaper CI.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Do not edit triggers yet. First classify whether the cost driver is runner SKU, run volume, duration, artifacts/storage, or repeated superseded runs.

trigger_signals.description: A proposed patch makes a workflow or job skip through paths, paths-ignore, branches, a job-level if, a reduced schedule, or concurrency.cancel-in-progress.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Before applying the patch, check required-check behavior and whether the skipped job is part of a safety boundary.

trigger_signals.description: The skipped or conditionally skipped job is a guard for labels, scope, import boundaries, security posture, release safety, dependency changes, or project architecture rules.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat the skip as semantics-changing until the guard's purpose and false-negative cases are understood.

trigger_signals.description: A timeout is shortened because recent runs seemed fast, without checking recent successful p90/max duration and variance.
trigger_signals.pattern: timeout-minutes|recent runs are fast|shorter timeout|runner timeout
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Use observed run-duration evidence and headroom rather than intuition before tightening timeout-minutes.

negative_signals.description: The workflow is not a required status check, has no safety or release semantics, and a skipped run is acceptable for the repository's documented policy.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The trap targets unsafe or unexamined skips. Optional advisory workflows can often use path or schedule reductions after ordinary review.

negative_signals.description: A required-check aggregator or explicit no-op success path preserves the required check for excluded changes.
negative_signals.pattern: required check aggregator|noop success|stub job|always reports success for skipped paths
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The required-check problem is about making the check disappear or remain pending. An intentional replacement signal can make path filtering safe.

negative_signals.description: The job-level condition only skips work after an unconditional safety wrapper has validated labels, scope, required files, and false-negative cases.
negative_signals.pattern: validated before skip|guard condition inside validation|unconditional wrapper
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Skipping expensive work after the safety decision is different from skipping the safety decision itself.

negative_signals.description: Recent successful run history shows the tighter timeout remains above observed max or high percentile with explicit headroom, and the next main run confirms it.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Timeout changes can be reasonable when they are evidence-based and verified, not guessed.

common_wrong_assumptions: If a docs-only pull request does not need full CI, it is always safe for the CI workflow not to start.
A job that normally no-ops can be skipped at the job level without changing the meaning of the safety guard.
Source-only path filters are enough for import-boundary, dependency, or security checks even when config files can change semantics.
A short timeout is safe because recent runs usually finish quickly, even without checking p90, max, variance, and the next main run.
Expensive runner types or matrix builds are always the cause of high Actions cost; run volume, cancellation policy, artifacts, and repeated reruns are secondary.
A concurrency group is harmless if it cancels old runs, even when the group name can collide across workflows, branches, or release jobs.

first_checks.check: Separate price multiplier from volume: inspect billing/usage, recent workflow run counts, runner types, durations, artifact/cache storage, and rerun/cancellation patterns before blaming a specific workflow or runner SKU.
first_checks.why: Cost can come from per-minute rates, run volume, storage, or repeated superseded runs; the safest optimization depends on the actual cost driver.
first_checks.command: Review GitHub billing/usage and recent Actions run history before editing workflow YAML.

first_checks.check: Check branch protection, rulesets, and required status checks before skipping an entire workflow with paths, paths-ignore, branches, or commit-message skip behavior.
first_checks.why: GitHub documents that workflows skipped by branch/path/message filters can leave associated checks pending, blocking protected-branch merges if those checks are required.
first_checks.command: Inspect repository branch protection/rulesets and required status check names, using the project's normal read-only settings/API path.

first_checks.check: For job-level if conditions on safety guards, identify what the guard is supposed to catch and whether absence or misuse of a label/scope marker is part of the risk.
first_checks.why: If unlabeled, mislabeled, or unexpected-scope pull requests are a failure mode, a job-level skip can make the guard invisible exactly when it should speak.

first_checks.check: For path filters on boundary, security, dependency, or import checks, include config surfaces that change semantics: package manifests, lockfiles, build/test config, tsconfig, lint/boundary config, module resolution config, action definitions, and workflow files.
first_checks.why: A source-only filter can miss changes that alter dependency resolution, imports, checks, or CI behavior without touching source files.

first_checks.check: Before reducing timeout-minutes, sample recent successful job durations and set a threshold above observed max or high percentile with headroom; verify on the next main/default-branch run.
first_checks.why: Timeouts are safety and reliability limits. A guessed timeout can convert slow-but-valid checks into flaky failures or hide real regression timing.
first_checks.command: Review recent job execution times in GitHub Actions run history or job usage views.

first_checks.check: Smoke-test an excluded-path pull request or dry-run equivalent and record which workflows start, skip, or report a replacement success signal.
first_checks.why: The observable result confirms whether the cost-saving edit preserved mergeability and required-check semantics.

decision_rules.condition: A proposed path, branch, or commit-message skip may affect a workflow whose check is required by branch protection or rulesets.
decision_rules.then: Do not make the required workflow disappear. Either keep it running, add a required-check aggregator/no-op success path that preserves the required signal, or route the required-check policy change through the repository's review/approval path.

decision_rules.condition: A job-level if would skip a guard whose purpose includes catching absent, wrong, or unexpected labels/scope/configuration.
decision_rules.then: Keep the safety guard visible, perform the cheap validation unconditionally, and only skip expensive subwork after the guard has made an explicit pass/skip/fail decision.

decision_rules.condition: A boundary, dependency, security, or import-check workflow is filtered only to source directories while config or dependency files can alter the checked semantics.
decision_rules.then: Include package manifests, lockfiles, build/test/lint/boundary config, module resolution config, action definitions, and workflow files that can change the check's meaning.

decision_rules.condition: The cost driver is repeated superseded pull-request runs and the workflow is not a release/deploy/ordered-state operation that must finish every run.
decision_rules.then: Prefer canceling superseded PR runs with a workflow-specific concurrency group, while avoiding group-name collisions across workflows, branches, release jobs, or environments that require ordered completion.

decision_rules.condition: A shorter timeout is proposed but recent duration evidence has not been sampled.
decision_rules.then: Collect recent successful job durations, choose a timeout above observed max or high percentile with headroom, and verify on the next main/default-branch run before claiming the optimization is safe.

decision_rules.condition: The workflow is optional, non-safety-critical, not required for protected branches, and the excluded paths cannot affect the workflow's semantics.
decision_rules.then: Proceed with normal workflow optimization review, while documenting which required-check and safety-boundary checks made the skip acceptable.

do_not: Do not make a required workflow disappear without preserving a required success signal or changing the requirement through the repository's approved path.
Do not skip label, scope, boundary, or security safety guards at the job level when that makes unlabeled, mislabeled, or config-only changes invisible.
Do not filter boundary checks only to source files when manifests, lockfiles, build config, lint config, workflow files, or module-resolution config can change the boundary.
Do not set timeout-minutes from intuition; use observed successful duration evidence and follow-up verification.
Do not use a broad concurrency group that can cancel unrelated workflows, release jobs, deploy jobs, or branches that must complete independently.
Do not report cost savings from workflow edits until required-check behavior and the next main/default-branch run have been checked.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Classify the workflow's cost driver and safety role, check required status checks/rulesets, then design the smallest cost reduction that preserves required-check signals and guard semantics.

risk.notes: Read-only cost analysis and local workflow drafting are low risk, but mutating shared CI, required status checks, release/deploy workflows, billing controls, or repository rules can affect mergeability, safety, availability, or cost. Route those mutations through the repository's review and approval path.

title: Human disagreement should trigger contrastive verification
summary: When a human collaborator says the agent’s diagnosis feels wrong, do not blindly agree or defend. Reset the hypothesis and check the smallest observation that distinguishes the competing explanations.
ai_value: Helps agents escape sycophancy, self-defense, and repeated retries by turning disagreement into a concrete verification plan.

contexts: a human says the agent is looking in the wrong place, misunderstanding a step, or missing old-system parity
the agent feels tempted to apologize without evidence or argue from its current theory
retries are consuming budget without a discriminating observation

trigger_signals.description: The human says “this feels wrong,” “the old system works,” or “you are checking the wrong step.”
trigger_signals.pattern: feels wrong|old system works|wrong step|not the issue
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Downgrade the current hypothesis to provisional and compare assumptions.

trigger_signals.description: The agent is about to repeat the same fix or produce a defensive explanation.
trigger_signals.pattern: retry|I still think|as I said|you are right
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Stop and design a discriminating observation first.

negative_signals.description: The human is making an explicit preference choice rather than a factual disagreement.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Treat it as preference or business judgment, not a diagnostic hypothesis.

negative_signals.description: The next check would cross a protected gate or cause irreversible effects.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Define stop conditions and use the required gate before checking.

common_wrong_assumptions: Human disagreement means the agent must immediately concede.
Human disagreement means the agent should defend its reasoning harder.
More retries are better than pausing to separate hypotheses.

first_checks.check: Write the human concern, the agent hypothesis, and the observation that would distinguish them.
first_checks.why: This prevents both blind deference and defensive inertia.

first_checks.check: Run the smallest safe check that separates the hypotheses.
first_checks.why: A direct observation is cheaper and more reliable than another broad retry.

first_checks.check: Report which hypothesis survived and what changed in the plan.
first_checks.why: The human sees evidence instead of apology theatre or argument.

decision_rules.condition: A human factual objection conflicts with the agent’s current diagnosis.
decision_rules.then: State that the current hypothesis is provisional, run the smallest safe differentiating check, then continue only from the evidence.

decision_rules.condition: The discriminating check would touch protected state.
decision_rules.then: Stop and route through the appropriate safety gate before touching protected state.

do_not: Do not answer disagreement with automatic capitulation.
Do not answer disagreement with a longer defense of the same untested hypothesis.
Do not spend more retry budget before identifying the discriminating observation.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Convert the disagreement into a two-hypothesis check, run the smallest safe observation, and report the surviving explanation.

title: L7 HTTP/1.1 keep-alive mismatches can look like phantom application 502s
summary: When an L7 load balancer or reverse proxy reuses upstream HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connections, a backend keep-alive idle timeout that is shorter than the proxy idle timeout can surface as intermittent proxy-side 502s while target-side 5xx and application logs remain clean.
ai_value: Helps debugging agents avoid chasing phantom route, handler, or database defects when the stronger hypothesis is a stale upstream connection race, while preserving boundaries around 503, 504, HTTP/2/gRPC, L4 load balancers, retry safety, and residual non-idle connection closes.

contexts: an agent is debugging intermittent gateway-side 502s from an L7 load balancer or reverse proxy that pools upstream HTTP/1.1 connections
load-balancer-generated 5xx counters rise while target-generated 5xx counters, application errors, restarts, and health checks remain clean
traffic is quiet or bursty enough that pooled upstream sockets can sit idle beyond the backend keep-alive timeout
the fix under consideration involves backend keep-alive, proxy upstream idle timeout, connection retries, or build/deploy assertions for timeout parity

tools.name: L7 load balancer or reverse proxy
tools.version_range: general HTTP/1.1 upstream keep-alive reuse pattern
observed_versions: de-identified 2026 production incident and provider-neutral reverse-proxy reasoning

tools.name: HTTP/1.1 backend server runtime
tools.version_range: general runtime keep-alive idle timeout pattern
observed_versions: de-identified backend keep-alive shorter than load-balancer idle timeout

trigger_signals.description: The dominant symptom is intermittent gateway-side 502 from an L7 proxy or load balancer, while target/application 5xx counters stay at or near zero.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Separate load-balancer-generated errors from target-generated errors before blaming application code.

trigger_signals.description: No matching handler exception, crash, restart, OOM, or route-specific failure appears for the same time window.
trigger_signals.pattern: no handler log|no exception|no restart|health checks green|target response normal
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Clean target evidence does not prove the load balancer is flaky; it raises the stale upstream connection hypothesis.

trigger_signals.description: Failures correlate with idle gaps or bursty traffic rather than raw request volume or one specific endpoint.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The likely driver is a reused idle upstream connection whose backend-side lifetime ended first.

trigger_signals.description: The deployed backend keep-alive idle timeout is shorter than, equal to, or only barely greater than the load-balancer/proxy upstream idle timeout.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Check the inequality with units and margin against live infrastructure and deployed runtime values, not only source defaults.

trigger_signals.description: Direct evidence shows a backend FIN or RST on a reused connection, or load-balancer/proxy access logs report a target connection close/reset cause.
trigger_signals.pattern: FIN|RST|target closed|connection reset|upstream prematurely closed|tcpdump|access log reason
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: This is stronger evidence for a connection-lifetime race than metrics alone.

negative_signals.description: Target/application 5xx is non-zero, correlates with the alarm, or application logs show matching handler failures.
negative_signals.pattern: target 5xx non-zero|application error spike|handler exception|route failure
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A real target failure should be investigated before applying a stale-connection explanation.

negative_signals.description: The dominant code is 504 rather than 502.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: 504 commonly indicates backend slowness, response timeout, connect timeout, or missing response bytes, not this keep-alive reuse race.

negative_signals.description: The dominant code is 503 rather than 502.
negative_signals.pattern: 503|Service Unavailable|no healthy targets|no registered targets|capacity|surge queue
negative_signals.why_it_matters: 503 usually points to target availability, registration, readiness, capacity, or rejection conditions, not backend keep-alive parity.

negative_signals.description: The service is behind only an L4 load balancer or TCP pass-through path with no HTTP L7 proxy generating the response.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Pure L4 load balancers do not generate HTTP 502s from upstream HTTP keep-alive reuse; TCP resets or another HTTP component must be diagnosed instead.

negative_signals.description: The target protocol itself is HTTP/2 or gRPC, rather than client-to-proxy HTTP/2 with HTTP/1.1 upstream targets.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: HTTP/2/gRPC has different multiplexing, GOAWAY, stream, and ping-idle semantics; this HTTP/1.1 keep-alive race is not the default explanation.

negative_signals.description: The 502s line up with deploys, draining, deregistration delay, TLS handshake failures, malformed or oversized headers, security groups, network ACLs, or connectivity failures.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Those are independent causes of load-balancer-side 502s with clean target 5xx and should not be hidden by this trap.

common_wrong_assumptions: Zero target 5xx means the load balancer is flaky.
Every gateway-side 502 must come from a broken handler, route, or database dependency.
502, 503, and 504 are interchangeable load-balancer 5xx symptoms.
A backend keep-alive value that is greater by one millisecond is enough operational margin.
Setting the idle timeout parity eliminates every possible stale-connection race.
Retry is always safe because the request probably did not reach the application.
The source-code default is the deployed value, even if a build or base image changed it.
Client HTTP/2 or L4 load-balancer behavior has the same failure model as HTTP/1.1 upstream keep-alive reuse.

first_checks.check: Separate load-balancer-generated 5xx from target-generated 5xx over the same time window, and confirm the dominant status is 502.
first_checks.why: The trap depends on a clean-target 502 signature; collapsed 5xx metrics hide false positives.

first_checks.check: Read the live load-balancer or proxy upstream idle timeout, not only IaC or source configuration.
first_checks.why: The live setting can drift independently of code and is the value the deployed service must satisfy.

first_checks.check: Read the built/deployed backend runtime value for keep-alive idle timeout and convert units explicitly into backend_keepalive_ms.
first_checks.why: Build steps, runtime defaults, and environment variables can diverge from source defaults; unit mismatch is a common silent failure.

first_checks.check: Prove backend_keepalive_ms >= load_balancer_idle_timeout_ms + margin, where the margin is at least a few seconds unless the platform has a stronger documented requirement.
first_checks.why: A practical margin absorbs timer granularity, scheduling jitter, and near-boundary races better than a hairline greater-than check.

first_checks.check: Inspect load-balancer/proxy access logs and, when feasible, packet or socket evidence for backend FIN/RST on a reused connection.
first_checks.why: Direct connection-close evidence distinguishes this race from other clean-target 502 causes.

first_checks.check: Check whether upstream connection-failure retries are enabled only for idempotent requests, and whether non-idempotent methods have explicit idempotency handling before retry.
first_checks.why: Retries can mask this race safely for idempotent requests but can duplicate non-idempotent work.

decision_rules.condition: The error is an L7 HTTP/1.1 gateway-side 502 with clean target/application 5xx and backend_keepalive_ms is below load_balancer_idle_timeout_ms plus margin.
decision_rules.then: Raise backend keep-alive above the proxy idle timeout or lower the proxy idle timeout below backend keep-alive, then enforce the inequality in build and deploy checks.

decision_rules.condition: The runtime is managed or backend keep-alive cannot be configured safely, but the proxy/LB idle timeout can be reduced without violating service requirements.
decision_rules.then: Lower the load-balancer/proxy upstream idle timeout below the deployed backend keep-alive value, preserving enough application timeout budget for legitimate long operations.

decision_rules.condition: The timeout inequality is already satisfied with margin but 502s continue and direct evidence shows connection closes around request dispatch.
decision_rules.then: Investigate max-requests-per-connection, maximum connection lifetime, worker recycle, shutdown, deploy/drain behavior, and proxy retry handling rather than declaring the timeout fix failed.

decision_rules.condition: The proposed mitigation is retrying failed upstream connection attempts.
decision_rules.then: Enable or rely on retries only for idempotent requests or where explicit idempotency keys/deduplication make duplicate execution safe; otherwise escalate before changing retry behavior.

decision_rules.condition: The dominant symptom is 503, 504, L4/TCP reset, target HTTP/2/gRPC behavior, or deploy/draining/TLS/header/connectivity evidence.
decision_rules.then: Do not apply the HTTP/1.1 upstream keep-alive mismatch trap; diagnose the observed status, protocol, and platform-specific cause directly.

do_not: Do not debug only individual routes when load-balancer-side 502s occur with zero target-side 5xx and clean application logs.
Do not treat 503 or 504 as this trap without status-specific evidence; they usually indicate different systems.
Do not compare seconds to milliseconds without explicit conversion and a margin.
Do not rely only on build-time constants when the live load-balancer or proxy setting can drift.
Do not claim the timeout inequality eliminates all stale-connection races; max request count, max lifetime, shutdown, and deploy/drain can still close connections.
Do not blanket-retry non-idempotent requests unless duplicate execution is handled by idempotency keys or another reviewed mechanism.
Do not include private service names, internal URLs, account identifiers, incident identifiers, bucket names, wrapper names, or organization-specific tooling in public lessons.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: First classify the status/protocol boundary, then read live proxy idle timeout and deployed backend keep-alive values, prove backend_keepalive_ms >= load_balancer_idle_timeout_ms + margin, and change only the timeout/retry lever that is safe for the service's idempotency and runtime constraints.

risk.notes: Diagnosis and read-only checks are safe, but changing production load-balancer timeout or retry policy can affect live availability and non-idempotent request semantics. Public publication also requires public-safety review; this candidate is de-identified and source-backed but should not authorize live mutation by itself.

sources.supports: AWS Application Load Balancer troubleshooting distinguishes load-balancer-generated HTTP 502 from target-generated errors and lists target FIN/RST while a request is outstanding, including checking whether target keep-alive is shorter than load-balancer idle timeout.

AWS Application Load Balancer attributes document connection idle timeout, recommend application idle timeout larger than load-balancer idle timeout, and distinguish connection idle timeout from HTTP client keepalive duration.

title: Lock the shared resource, not only the artifact
summary: A lock scoped to artifact or request identity prevents duplicate submissions of the same artifact but does not stop two different artifacts from concurrently mutating and superseding one shared resource.
ai_value: Helps deployment, publication, import, and migration agents choose lock granularity that protects the mutable target for the full mutation-plus-verification window.

contexts: operations mutate one shared downstream resource such as a deploy target, publication channel, import destination, migration target, or named environment
duplicate suppression is keyed by commit, image tag, filename, batch id, or request id
two different artifacts can be submitted concurrently

trigger_signals.description: Duplicate submissions of the same artifact are prevented, but two different artifacts still run concurrently.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The lock key protects artifact identity, not the shared resource.

trigger_signals.description: Both operations log success while final state reflects only one artifact.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Success is local to each mutation; final shared-resource state may have superseded one result.

trigger_signals.description: A follow-up attempt risks rolling back newer work by redeploying or republishing its own artifact.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Re-read current target and require forward-only reconciliation before retry.

trigger_signals.description: The test suite uses two copies of the same artifact but not two different artifacts for the same resource.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Same-artifact tests prove duplicate suppression only; add a two-artifact resource contention test.

negative_signals.description: Artifacts target disjoint resources.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Artifact-scoped suppression can be sufficient when there is no shared mutable target.

negative_signals.description: The downstream system enforces a forward-only compare-and-set or equivalent optimistic concurrency check on the shared resource.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Resource-wide locking is one safety design; a strong CAS can be the alternative with better throughput.

negative_signals.description: Head-of-line blocking would be worse than the risk and optimistic forward-only reconciliation is already enforced and tested.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Resource-wide locks trade throughput for safety; choose deliberately.

common_wrong_assumptions: A lock keyed by commit, tag, filename, or batch id protects the deployment or import target.
If both operations log success, both outcomes are still reflected.
Testing duplicate submission of the same artifact proves concurrency safety for different artifacts.

first_checks.check: Identify the mutable resource that must be single-writer for the whole mutation plus verification window.
first_checks.why: The lock key should match the hazard, not merely the request identity.

first_checks.check: Run a concurrency test with two different artifacts targeting the same resource.
first_checks.why: This is the discriminator that same-artifact duplicate tests miss.

first_checks.check: Assert the second operation waits or refuses before downstream mutation, and that release wakes only the next eligible waiter.
first_checks.why: Ordering must be enforced before the shared target changes.

first_checks.check: Re-read current target before retry and require forward-only reconciliation from the state observed at acquisition.
first_checks.why: Retries must not roll back newer work.

decision_rules.condition: Two different artifacts can mutate the same target concurrently under an artifact-scoped lock.
decision_rules.then: Lock the shared resource for the full mutation and verification window, while keeping artifact-scoped duplicate suppression as a lower layer.

decision_rules.condition: The downstream target enforces forward-only compare-and-set on current state.
decision_rules.then: A resource-wide lock may be unnecessary; keep the CAS evidence and test two-artifact races.

decision_rules.condition: A contender waits for the shared resource lock.
decision_rules.then: Record holder, arrival, target metadata, and wake only the next eligible waiter after release.

do_not: Do not claim concurrency safety from same-artifact duplicate tests alone.
Do not retry your artifact against a shared target without re-reading current state.
Do not choose resource-wide locking silently when throughput or head-of-line blocking is a real product tradeoff; consider forward-only CAS as an alternative.

Do not include private service names, internal URLs, account identifiers, incident identifiers, private repository paths, tenant/store names, setup-card field names, low-level endpoint strings or organization-specific tooling in public lessons.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Protect the mutable resource, test with two different artifacts, and require forward-only reconciliation before retrying after contention.

title: Long-running probes need safe progress output
summary: A long-running diagnostic that stays silent makes it hard to tell normal slowness from a stuck process, runaway scope, or a probe approaching a safety boundary.
ai_value: Helps agents design diagnostic probes that remain observable, bounded, and safe for handoff without exposing sensitive data.

contexts: a diagnostic scans many records, files, pages, or remote responses
runtime is uncertain and another actor may need to decide whether to wait or stop
the probe is part of a safe halt or approval-sensitive investigation
progress evidence must be shareable without leaking sensitive values

tools.name: agent-workflow-orchestration
observed_versions: de-identified 2026 agent safety and recovery sessions

trigger_signals.description: The probe may run long enough that silence could be mistaken for a hang.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Define and emit a safe progress cadence before starting.

trigger_signals.description: The next decision depends on whether the probe is still within bounded read-only or dry-run scope.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Report phase, counts, elapsed time, and stop reasons without sensitive values.

trigger_signals.description: Another agent or human may take over while the probe is running.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Make progress output useful for wait, stop, or escalation decisions.

negative_signals.description: The command is short, deterministic, and completes before coordination uncertainty can arise.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Extra progress machinery may add noise when the operation is visibly bounded.

negative_signals.description: Progress output would require exposing sensitive records and the probe cannot aggregate safely.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Reduce the probe scope or redesign it before logging details.

negative_signals.description: The operation is a known long quiet phase such as emulated cross-architecture build work, and builder status or prior observed duration indicates progress.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Silence alone is not a stall; set no-output timeouts above observed duration and check builder status before killing the job.

common_wrong_assumptions: No errors means a long-running probe is still making progress.
Progress logs are only convenience, not safety evidence.
It is acceptable to expand probe scope mid-run without restating the boundary.

first_checks.check: State probe mode before launch: read-only, dry-run, or mutating.
first_checks.why: Mode controls whether the agent may proceed or must stop at a gate.

first_checks.check: Define a progress cadence such as every fixed count, phase, or time interval.
first_checks.why: A cadence makes stalls visible without guesswork.

first_checks.check: Emit only aggregate progress and safe stop reasons.
first_checks.why: Aggregate breadcrumbs preserve observability without leaking sensitive data.

first_checks.check: For known quiet build phases, check builder status and observed duration before killing for no output.
first_checks.why: This distinguishes legitimate silence from a stuck probe.

decision_rules.condition: The probe can report aggregate progress safely.
decision_rules.then: Run the bounded probe and emit phase, count, elapsed time, and stop-condition breadcrumbs.

decision_rules.condition: The probe cannot report progress without exposing sensitive data.
decision_rules.then: Reduce scope or redesign logging until progress can be public-safe or appropriately restricted.

decision_rules.condition: Progress stalls past the expected cadence or approaches a mutation, availability, permission, cost, or data-loss boundary.
decision_rules.then: Stop or inspect with read-only process evidence before continuing.

do_not: Do not run a silent probe over uncertain scope.
Do not expose sensitive records in progress logs.
Do not treat lack of errors as evidence of progress.
Do not extend scope mid-run without making the new boundary explicit.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Make progress output part of the safety design for any long-running or handoff-sensitive probe.

title: Mechanical migrations need enforced target state
summary: Large-surface migrations are not done because search and review look clean. Define the target state mechanically, ban old shapes in scope, keep allowlists small, and run checks that prove the migration cannot silently regress.
ai_value: Helps agents finish theme, API, schema, naming, and other broad migrations with enforceable checks instead of relying on eyeballing rare paths.

contexts: a migration replaces fixed values, old APIs, deprecated names, or scattered patterns across many files
some surfaces are rarely visited or generated
a sibling checkout, stale branch, or partial implementation could reintroduce the old shape

trigger_signals.description: Review says the migration is complete but there is no lint, test, or generator enforcing the new shape.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat completion as fragile until the old pattern is mechanically banned in scope.

trigger_signals.description: An allowlist exists but has broad paths or unexplained exceptions.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Shrink and explain exceptions so they remain debt, not silent permission.

negative_signals.description: The migration is a one-file obvious rename with a compiler-enforced failure on old usage.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A lighter check may be enough.

negative_signals.description: The old shape intentionally remains supported as public compatibility.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then the target state is coexistence; tests should state the boundary.

common_wrong_assumptions: Search-and-replace plus review is enough for broad migrations.
Allowlisted exceptions prove the migration is complete.
A clean current checkout means stale sibling branches cannot reintroduce old shapes.

first_checks.check: Define the target state and the old patterns banned in the migration scope.
first_checks.why: A check needs an explicit forbidden set and scope.

first_checks.check: Add or run a mechanical check for banned patterns and undefined new references.
first_checks.why: This catches rare screens and stale generated surfaces.

first_checks.check: Inspect related checkouts or branches before handoff when they may reintroduce the old shape.
first_checks.why: Operational residue can undo a correct migration after merge.

decision_rules.condition: A broad migration lacks mechanical enforcement for the target state.
decision_rules.then: Add a scoped lint/test/generator check or keep the migration incomplete with explicit debt.

decision_rules.condition: Exceptions are needed.
decision_rules.then: Keep exceptions narrow, path-specific, and documented with follow-up criteria.

do_not: Do not declare broad migration complete from search results alone.
Do not use broad allowlists as proof of completion.
Do not ignore stale sibling checkouts that can reintroduce the old shape.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Turn the desired migration state into a scoped mechanical check, explain any allowlist, and verify related checkout residue before handoff.

title: Move UI date logic instead of weakening the guard
summary: When a UI guard rejects inline date construction or formatting, the fix is usually to move date-sensitive logic to the approved helper or boundary, not to broaden the exception until the warning disappears.
ai_value: Helps agents fix hydration, locale, timezone, and deterministic-rendering problems without silencing the project rule that was created to prevent them.

contexts: browser-rendered UI source has a guard against inline date/time constructors or formatters
the change computes today, local dates, relative labels, or formatted timestamps near render code
the project already has helper, server-side, or explicit client-local display patterns

trigger_signals.description: A lint, CI, or review guard flags date/time construction or formatting inside UI rendering code.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Move the logic to the approved layer before considering a guard exception.

trigger_signals.description: The UI change computes today, local date labels, or timezone-sensitive text directly in a component.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Check existing date-display patterns for deterministic or intentionally client-local rendering.

negative_signals.description: The component is explicitly the approved client-local date display boundary.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The guard may not apply if this is the documented boundary.

negative_signals.description: The value is static build-time content with no locale or timezone behavior.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Inline rendering may be acceptable under project rules.

common_wrong_assumptions: The fastest fix is to add another exception to the guard.
Date formatting near the UI is harmless if tests pass locally.
Hydration and timezone problems can be reviewed later.

first_checks.check: Find the project-approved date helper, server-side formatter, or client-local display component.
first_checks.why: Using the existing boundary preserves the rule instead of weakening it.

first_checks.check: Move the date-only or timezone-sensitive logic to that boundary.
first_checks.why: The UI component should receive a safe value or intentionally client-local display wrapper.

first_checks.check: Rerun the failing guard and the relevant UI/unit tests.
first_checks.why: Passing both proves the architecture and behavior survived the move.

decision_rules.condition: A guard flags inline date/time logic in ordinary browser-rendered UI.
decision_rules.then: Move the logic into the existing helper/server/client-local pattern, then rerun the guard.

decision_rules.condition: No approved boundary exists and the feature truly needs client-local time.
decision_rules.then: Create or review a narrow display pattern rather than weakening the broad guard.

do_not: Do not broaden a UI date/time guard before trying to move the logic.
Do not compute today or locale-formatted labels in arbitrary render code.
Do not claim the fix is safe without rerunning the guard that failed.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Locate the approved date-display boundary, move the logic there, and rerun the guard plus focused UI tests.

risk.notes: Code movement is usually low risk; weakening guards can reintroduce hydration and timezone defects.

title: Moved UI tests need absence and presence assertions
summary: When a UI item moves from one navigation or menu surface to another, a destination-only test can miss duplicates left behind. Prove both presence in the new place and absence from the old one.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid partial UI move verification where a component appears in the new location but stale source-surface rendering or expectations remain.

contexts: a navigation item, menu entry, button, link, or panel moves between UI surfaces
separate components or tests render the old and new surfaces
the visible diff touches one component but related tests still encode old grouping

trigger_signals.description: A test or snapshot only asserts the item appears in its new surface.
trigger_signals.pattern: appears in new location|destination test|navigation move
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Add a source-surface absence assertion before calling the move complete.

trigger_signals.description: CI fails in a related menu/sidebar/nav test that was not edited.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat it as evidence that the move spans multiple surfaces.

trigger_signals.description: The UI test runs against shared or pre-seeded state where unrelated visible rows may already exist.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Use both presence and absence assertions and seed an extra unrelated row to prove the test checks the intended contract.

negative_signals.description: The old surface is deleted entirely and no other component can render it.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Absence may be covered by removal, but still check imports/routes for stale render paths.

negative_signals.description: The move is intentionally a duplication or cross-list alias.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then tests should state both expected locations explicitly.

common_wrong_assumptions: If the new location test passes, the old location cannot still show the item.
Only the component touched in the diff needs tests.
Snapshot failures in old surfaces are unrelated cleanup.

first_checks.check: Identify every UI surface that can render the moved item.
first_checks.why: Moves often cross component boundaries; the source and destination both need evidence.

first_checks.check: Run or add paired assertions for source absence and destination presence.
first_checks.why: This catches both missing moves and accidental duplicates.

first_checks.check: Review queries or snapshots for stale labels and grouping assumptions.
first_checks.why: Old test expectations can preserve the pre-move model even when the UI changed intentionally.

first_checks.check: Seed or identify an extra unrelated visible row and confirm the test still validates the intended moved item.
first_checks.why: This proves the assertion is not merely counting any visible row in shared state.

decision_rules.condition: The item should move, not duplicate.
decision_rules.then: Update tests so the destination contains the item and the source no longer does.

decision_rules.condition: The item should intentionally appear in both places.
decision_rules.then: Make both presence assertions explicit and name the product reason for duplication.

do_not: Do not verify a move with destination-only assertions.
Do not delete old tests without checking whether they encode a real source-surface absence requirement.
Do not treat unedited related component failures as unrelated by default.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Run the source and destination surface tests together and assert both absence and presence for the moved item.

risk.notes: Focused UI test changes are low risk; product decisions about intentional duplication may need normal review.
