title: Session-bound API broker expiry is an authorization boundary
summary: When a scoped API broker or session cache expires during long-running agent work, the safe action is to preserve completed work and stop external calls until the approved broker/bootstrap path is repaired, not to bypass the broker or claim the remaining batch completed.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid turning a read-only session failure into an authorization, secrecy, or provenance incident by switching to raw credentials, alternate endpoints, or overbroad retries after the approved broker state expires.

contexts: an agent is using a local broker, scoped API proxy, session cache, or bearer-exchange wrapper for external reads
earlier broker-mediated calls succeeded in the same long-running batch
a later broker call reports an invalid, expired, revoked, missing, or not-exchanged session
the remaining work needs external access but completed local analysis or artifacts can still be preserved

trigger_signals.description: The approved broker reports that its session or bearer is invalid, expired, revoked, missing, or not exchanged.
trigger_signals.pattern: invalid session|expired session|revoked session|not exchanged|missing bearer|session cache
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat this as an authorization boundary, not as permission to switch to raw credentials or a lower-level client.

trigger_signals.description: A broker renew/status command fails with the same authentication or session-state category.
trigger_signals.pattern: renew failed|status failed|rebootstrap required|login required|session repair required
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Stop external calls and hand off the exact restart point through the approved bootstrap flow.

trigger_signals.description: The agent has partially completed a batch and is tempted to keep going through a different path because the operation is read-only.
trigger_signals.pattern: read-only|direct client|raw credential|alternate endpoint|continue batch|remaining calls
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Read-only intent does not remove the authorization boundary; preserve completed local artifacts and mark the remaining external portion blocked.

negative_signals.description: The failure is clearly input validation or a malformed request while broker authentication remains healthy.
negative_signals.pattern: 400 bad request|schema validation|missing required field|invalid input
negative_signals.why_it_matters: This trap is about expired or invalid authorization/session state. Normal request validation failures should be fixed at the request level.

negative_signals.description: The approved broker/bootstrap flow has already been repaired and the same scoped access path is working again.
negative_signals.pattern: session renewed|broker healthy|bootstrap complete|scoped access restored
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Once approved broker access is restored, the agent can resume through that same boundary instead of remaining blocked.

negative_signals.description: The remaining work is purely local and does not need external access, secrets, private APIs, or account-scoped data.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Local analysis can continue safely if it does not depend on the expired authorization context.

negative_signals.description: The broker session is healthy, but the downstream provider returns a scoped 401 or 403 for a specific resource.
negative_signals.pattern: broker healthy|session valid|provider 401|provider 403|permission denied for resource
negative_signals.why_it_matters: This may be a provider-side permission, resource-scope, or policy issue rather than expired broker state. Stay within the broker boundary and diagnose the provider response without bypassing authorization controls.

common_wrong_assumptions: Because the intended operation is read-only, bypassing the broker with raw credentials is harmless.
A lower-level API client is equivalent to the approved broker path if it reaches the same data.
The agent can keep retrying or broaden the data request until the missing calls are recovered.
A partially completed external batch can be reported as complete if the blocker appears late.
Debugging an expired broker session justifies printing, inspecting, or moving secrets.

first_checks.check: Run the broker's status or renew command once only if its documented contract is not to print secrets.
first_checks.why: A safe status/renew check can distinguish transient session state from permanent blocker without exposing credentials.

first_checks.check: Classify whether the error is authorization/session state rather than request validation or network flakiness.
first_checks.why: The next action differs: session-state failures stop external calls; malformed requests can be corrected within the approved path.

first_checks.check: Inventory completed local artifacts and the exact remaining external work without copying secrets, tokens, private URLs, raw payloads, or credentials.
first_checks.why: Preserving progress lets a later session resume safely after re-bootstrap without losing evidence or leaking sensitive data.

decision_rules.condition: The approved broker reports expired, invalid, revoked, or not-exchanged session state, and renewal through the approved path does not restore scoped access.
decision_rules.then: Stop all external calls, preserve completed local work, mark the remaining external batch blocked on approved re-bootstrap or session repair, and hand off the precise restart point.

decision_rules.condition: Some local analysis can continue without external access or secret-bearing data.
decision_rules.then: Continue only the local/offline portion, clearly separating completed local artifacts from blocked external reads.

decision_rules.condition: The agent is considering raw credentials, alternate endpoints, provider consoles, or broader data requests to bypass the failed broker.
decision_rules.then: Do not bypass the broker. Record the blocker category and route through the approved owner/session/bootstrap path before resuming external access.

do_not: Do not print, inspect, copy, or move secrets while debugging the broker session.
Do not bypass the broker with raw provider credentials, alternate endpoints, provider consoles, or lower-level clients unless a new approved path explicitly authorizes it.
Do not silently broaden the data request to compensate for missed calls.
Do not mark the unrun external portion complete.
Do not discard completed local analysis just because the external batch is blocked.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Run one safe broker status/renew check if available, then stop external calls on session-state failure, preserve completed work, and hand off the exact re-bootstrap requirement.

risk.notes: Expired broker state can involve auth, secrets, account access, confidentiality, and permission boundaries. This candidate supports safe stopping and handoff; it does not authorize credential handling or bypass.

title: Session boundaries need state reconciliation
summary: At the start or end of a stateful agent session, reconcile current files, branches, runtime state, and task status. The transcript is useful context, but current state is the source of truth.
ai_value: Helps agents recover from session death, long handoffs, and end-of-session fade-outs by leaving and reading restartable evidence instead of trusting stale memory.

contexts: a previous agent session crashed, timed out, or handed off mid-task
an agent is ending a session that changed files, branches, reviews, builds, or task state
the next action depends on whether code is complete, merged, deployed, verified, or merely attempted

trigger_signals.description: A handoff says work is done but current files, branches, tests, or runtime have not been inspected.
trigger_signals.pattern: handoff says done|session died|transcript says|not inspected
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat the handoff as a lead; verify current state before acting.

trigger_signals.description: A session is about to end after touching durable state.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Sweep current state and leave exact restart evidence.

negative_signals.description: The work was read-only and produced no durable state or follow-up.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A brief final note may be enough.

negative_signals.description: A dedicated workflow engine already recorded terminal state and artifact evidence.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Still verify if the next action is risky, but do not duplicate ceremony blindly.

common_wrong_assumptions: The last confident message in the transcript is the current truth.
If a session ends, cleanup will happen automatically.
Code-complete, pushed, merged, live, and verified are the same state.

first_checks.check: Inspect repository status, recent commits, task status, and relevant runtime/check state before resuming.
first_checks.why: This prevents stale transcript assumptions from driving the next action.

first_checks.check: Before ending, record what is code-complete, pushed, merged, deployed, smoke-tested, and still blocked.
first_checks.why: These are different states; future agents need the distinctions.

first_checks.check: Leave a next-safe-action that names the exact restart point.
first_checks.why: A restartable session boundary reduces duplicate investigation and accidental cleanup.

decision_rules.condition: A session starts from a crash or old handoff.
decision_rules.then: Inspect current state and reconcile it with the transcript before editing or reporting completion.

decision_rules.condition: A session is ending after durable changes.
decision_rules.then: Record file/branch/check/task state and next safe action before releasing the work.

do_not: Do not resume from chat memory without checking current state.
Do not collapse attempted, code-complete, merged, deployed, and verified into “done.”
Do not leave the next agent to infer restart state from silence.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: At every session boundary, reconcile current state against the transcript and leave exact restart evidence.

title: Shared authenticated browser contexts need page leases
summary: When browser automations share authenticated state, feature jobs should lease pages or tabs from a provider-owned context instead of closing the shared context from consumer cleanup.
ai_value: Helps agents prevent overlapping UI automations from killing each other while preserving narrow concurrency around provider-side jobs and authenticated-session lifecycle.

contexts: scheduled or parallel browser automations reuse a saved login, storage state, profile, or authenticated context
feature code receives browser context or page objects and owns cleanup
external provider UI operations overlap in time

trigger_signals.description: One browser job closes a context or browser shortly before a sibling job reports a closed page, closed context, navigation abort, or unknown browser crash.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Suspect consumer-owned cleanup of a shared authenticated resource.

trigger_signals.description: Feature callers receive a shared context or page and call close in their own cleanup.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Move lifecycle ownership back to the session provider and expose per-job leases.

trigger_signals.description: A proposed fix serializes all browser automation because one provider-side report or download is ambiguous.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Separate page/context sharing from the narrow provider job that may need its own mutex.

negative_signals.description: Each automation owns a fresh isolated browser profile or context and no authenticated state is shared.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The lease/refcount pattern is less relevant when there is no shared lifecycle.

negative_signals.description: The external provider requires full serial execution for every operation and that contract is documented.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: In that case a broader queue may be correct, though mutation readback still matters.

common_wrong_assumptions: Sharing a saved login means sharing one page is safe.
The caller that acquired a context may close the whole context on cleanup.
Serializing every browser job is the only durable fix.
If an edited field still shows the typed value, the provider accepted the mutation.

first_checks.check: Build an overlap timeline for acquisition, page creation, provider requests, cleanup, context close, and sibling failure.
first_checks.why: The timeline distinguishes browser lifecycle bugs from provider-side concurrency limits.

first_checks.check: Audit cleanup ownership: consumers release page leases; the provider owns context and browser retirement.
first_checks.why: A lease boundary prevents one job from killing another job’s authenticated state.

first_checks.check: Verify external mutation by reload, reopen, or provider-rendered readback.
first_checks.why: Reading the same edited DOM can confirm only local typing, not provider acceptance.

decision_rules.condition: Multiple automations share authenticated browser state.
decision_rules.then: Return a new page or tab lease per automation, refcount active leases, and close the shared context only when the provider-owned retirement policy allows it.

decision_rules.condition: Only one provider-side report, download, or mutation is ambiguous while other page flows are independent.
decision_rules.then: Protect the ambiguous provider job with a narrow mutex rather than serializing unrelated browser flows.

do_not: Do not hand the same page object to independent automations.
Do not let feature cleanup close a shared authenticated context or browser.
Do not log cookies, storage state, raw provider payloads, or credentials while diagnosing.
Do not infer provider acceptance from the same editable DOM after typing.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Put authenticated browser lifecycle behind a provider-owned session manager and give feature jobs lease-scoped pages with explicit release semantics.

risk.notes: This record concerns browser automation safety. It does not authorize bypassing provider terms, credential handling rules, or external mutation gates.

sources.supports: Claude and Gemini both identified the page-lease boundary as a novel public-worthy trap, with a caveat to include a neutral reproducer.

verification_runs.conclusion: The lifecycle failure is reproducible without provider-specific details.

title: Smoke tests must use the real user plane
summary: A smoke probe from the operator host can be a network-topology signal rather than service-health evidence. Keep a smoke path through the same plane real users use.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid both false-down and false-up conclusions when private networks, meshes, proxies, or gateways separate operator reachability from user reachability.

contexts: a service is reachable through a user gateway, proxy, mesh, or public edge but not necessarily from the operator host
a private address, internal hostname, or side-channel probe is used for smoke testing
a rollout or auth migration needs evidence from the actual user path

trigger_signals.description: An operator-host probe times out against a private or internal address.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat it as topology evidence until the real user plane is tested.

trigger_signals.description: A side-channel health check succeeds while user-path requests fail.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Do not call the service healthy until the real gateway or user plane passes.

trigger_signals.description: The smoke test bypasses auth, routing, proxy, or gateway layers that real users traverse.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Add a redacted real-plane smoke that exercises those layers safely.

negative_signals.description: The operator host is intentionally inside the same network and auth plane as users.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then the probe may be representative, but document why.

negative_signals.description: The task only needs a component liveness check, not user-visible readiness.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A side-channel health check can be useful if it is not overclaimed.

common_wrong_assumptions: Timeout from my shell means the service is down.
A private health endpoint passing means users can reach the service.
Smoke tests can ignore the gateway because routing was not changed.

first_checks.check: Draw or list the operator plane, service plane, and real user plane for the smoke path.
first_checks.why: Reachability depends on topology, not just process health.

first_checks.check: Run a redacted smoke through the same gateway or user-facing path real users use.
first_checks.why: This catches false-up side-channel health and false-down operator reachability.

first_checks.check: Record what the smoke proves and what it bypasses.
first_checks.why: Evidence labels prevent topology signals from being mistaken for health truth.

decision_rules.condition: Operator-plane probe fails but real-plane status is unknown.
decision_rules.then: Do not call the service down; test through the real user plane or inspect routing.

decision_rules.condition: Side-channel health passes but user plane fails.
decision_rules.then: Investigate the layers bypassed by the health check.

decision_rules.condition: Real-plane smoke passes and side-channel health passes.
decision_rules.then: Record both component liveness and user-path readiness.

do_not: Do not equate operator-host reachability with user reachability.
Do not overclaim side-channel health checks as user-visible readiness.
Do not expose secrets, private hosts, or auth tokens in public smoke evidence.

title: Split risky release work from routine cleanup
summary: When one closeout instruction bundles a high-attention release or gate with routine hygiene, the risky step consumes the evidence budget and cleanup becomes vague or skipped.
ai_value: Helps agents preserve both safety and hygiene by separating gated release evidence from routine cleanup evidence.

contexts: a closeout request includes a release, deploy, publication, or other high-attention step plus cleanup tasks
the release evidence is detailed but branch, artifact, draft, or temporary-file cleanup gets one unverified sentence
a failed or gated release step blocks unrelated cleanup that could safely finish

trigger_signals.description: One instruction mixes a gated release action with low-risk cleanup hygiene.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Split the work into separately verifiable units before starting.

trigger_signals.description: The report contains detailed release evidence but only claims cleanup happened.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Cleanup evidence is under-specified and should be checked directly.

trigger_signals.description: A blocked risky step leaves safe cleanup residues untouched.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Close the independent cleanup lane rather than letting the gate consume the whole task.

negative_signals.description: Cleanup is inseparable from the gated action and would change the same protected state.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then cleanup must wait behind the same gate.

negative_signals.description: The release step is purely local and reversible with no extra attention load.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Simple local tasks may not need formal separation.

common_wrong_assumptions: Closeout is one thing, so one evidence line can cover all of it.
If the release is blocked, cleanup must be blocked too.
Routine cleanup can be inferred from a successful deploy or publish.

first_checks.check: List gated/risky steps and routine cleanup steps separately before execution.
first_checks.why: Separate lists preserve attention and verification quality.

first_checks.check: Record evidence for cleanup independently, such as empty pending directory, clean git status, or archived draft manifest.
first_checks.why: Cleanup completion should not depend on release confidence.

first_checks.check: If the risky step blocks, complete safe independent cleanup or record why it is coupled.
first_checks.why: This prevents risk gates from creating unrelated residue.

decision_rules.condition: A release/gated action and routine cleanup are bundled.
decision_rules.then: Create separate checklist/evidence rows for the release and cleanup portions.

decision_rules.condition: The risky action blocks but cleanup is independent.
decision_rules.then: Complete or archive the cleanup lane and report the gated action separately.

decision_rules.condition: Cleanup would mutate the same protected state as the release.
decision_rules.then: Do not perform that cleanup until the protected action is authorized.

do_not: Do not let deploy or publication evidence stand in for cleanup evidence.
Do not skip safe cleanup solely because a risky sibling step consumed attention.
Do not hide coupled cleanup behind a generic “done” statement.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Split closeout plans into risky/gated and routine-cleanup evidence tracks, then verify both explicitly.

title: Stale CI aggregates need run-level evidence
summary: Aggregate CI status can lag or disagree with underlying workflow runs after merges and transitions. Before waiting, failing, or reporting success, inspect the concrete run conclusions, URLs, IDs, and timestamps.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid unnecessary waiting loops and false status reports when a pull request or branch aggregate is stale but individual CI runs have already concluded.

contexts: a pull request, branch, or merge queue aggregate shows pending, stale, or inconsistent CI status
individual workflow runs or jobs may have newer conclusions than the aggregate
an agent is deciding whether to wait, rerun, merge, deploy, or report a block

trigger_signals.description: Aggregate check status remains pending or stale after a workflow run appears complete.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Inspect the underlying run details before declaring a block.

trigger_signals.description: Different CI surfaces disagree about the same commit or pull request.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Prefer concrete run IDs and timestamps as evidence.

negative_signals.description: Underlying runs are also pending, queued, or missing for the target commit.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Waiting or triggering the expected run may be correct.

negative_signals.description: A required check is genuinely absent because a workflow was skipped by path, branch, or policy filters.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: That is a required-check semantics problem, not just aggregate lag.

common_wrong_assumptions: The aggregate status is always fresher than the workflow run page.
A pending aggregate means no useful CI evidence exists.
A green individual job means the required check policy is satisfied without checking the target commit.

first_checks.check: Open or query the individual workflow runs for the exact target commit.
first_checks.why: Run-level conclusion and timestamp reveal whether the aggregate is merely stale.

first_checks.check: Record run conclusion, run URL or ID, and completion timestamp in the gate evidence.
first_checks.why: Concrete evidence prevents vague "CI seems stuck" reports.

first_checks.check: Compare required-check names against the runs you inspected.
first_checks.why: A completed run only satisfies the gate if it corresponds to the required check for the target commit.

decision_rules.condition: Aggregate status is stale but underlying required runs for the exact target commit have succeeded.
decision_rules.then: Report the run-level evidence and refresh/retry the aggregate query before waiting longer.

decision_rules.condition: Aggregate is pending because required runs are skipped or absent.
decision_rules.then: Do not bypass the gate; inspect workflow trigger/required-check configuration through the normal review path.

do_not: Do not wait indefinitely on a stale aggregate without checking underlying runs.
Do not report CI green from an underlying run unless it matches the exact target commit and required check.
Do not bypass required checks because an aggregate UI looks confused.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Compare the aggregate with underlying workflow run conclusions, URLs/IDs, and timestamps for the exact target commit before deciding.

risk.notes: Read-only CI inspection is low risk. Reruns, required-check changes, and merge/deploy decisions follow normal gates.

title: Stale local readers can masquerade as broken credentials
summary: After a local state-file schema changes, an older sibling shell, daemon, or agent process may fail to parse the same state that newer tools can read. Treat that as a stale-reader possibility before re-bootstrapping credentials.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid unnecessary credential resets, token exposure risk, and operator interruption when the real fix is refreshing wrapper code or restarting a long-lived reader.

contexts: a local state or session file recently gained a new schema version
one process can read or renew local state while another reports an unsupported schema or parse failure
wrappers, symlinks, background daemons, MCP servers, or agent sessions may still be running old reader code

trigger_signals.description: One process succeeds against the local state while another fails with a schema, version, or parse error.
trigger_signals.pattern: schema version|unsupported schema|parse failed|one session succeeds|one session fails
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Compare reader versions before treating the state as corrupt or credentials as expired.

trigger_signals.description: The failing process is long-lived or launched from an older wrapper, symlink target, checkout, or daemon.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Refresh or restart the reader path before asking for new credentials.

negative_signals.description: All readers at the same version fail with an explicit authorization or revocation error.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: That points to a real credential/session problem rather than only a stale reader.

negative_signals.description: The state file was manually edited, truncated, or fails an integrity check in every reader.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Handle state corruption directly; refreshing code alone may not recover it.

common_wrong_assumptions: A schema parse error from one process proves the credentials are broken.
If one shell fails, every active reader must be using the same code.
Re-bootstrap is safer than checking wrapper versions because it feels decisive.

first_checks.check: Run the token-safe status or validation command from a freshly updated reader.
first_checks.why: This proves whether the newer reader can parse and renew the same local state without printing secrets.
first_checks.command: project-approved status command; do not print token material

first_checks.check: Compare the failing process launch path, wrapper version, symlink target, and start time with the working reader.
first_checks.why: A version or launch-path mismatch explains why two processes disagree about the same state.
first_checks.command: check process metadata and wrapper/version output

first_checks.check: Restart stale long-lived readers after updating wrapper code, then retry the same redacted status check.
first_checks.why: The correct fix should make the stale-reader error disappear without credential replacement.
files: daemon or MCP server restart evidence

decision_rules.condition: A newer reader succeeds but an older long-lived process fails on schema/version parsing.
decision_rules.then: Refresh the wrapper/checkout/symlink target, restart stale processes, and retry the token-safe status command before requesting new credentials.

decision_rules.condition: All refreshed readers fail with the same credential-specific authorization error.
decision_rules.then: Stop at the normal credential/session recovery boundary and preserve only redacted evidence.

do_not: Do not print or copy token material while comparing reader behavior.
Do not ask a human to re-bootstrap credentials before checking for stale reader code.
Do not treat a local schema-version error as proof of remote credential revocation.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Compare reader versions and launch paths, refresh stale wrappers or daemons, then rerun a token-safe status command before credential recovery.

risk.notes: Read-only version and status checks are low risk. Credential re-bootstrap or secret handling remains gated.

sources.excerpt: A stale process can report unsupported schema or parse failure while a refreshed reader handles the same local state successfully; credential re-bootstrap should be a later fallback.

title: Stale reference sweeps need live-vs-historical triage
summary: After a docs or knowledge-surface migration, deterministic stale-reference sweeps across live hooks, validators, profiles, prompts, docs, and CI must classify live references separately from historical evidence.
ai_value: Helps agents finish migrations without leaving old slugs in active operating surfaces or destroying audit history by overzealous cleanup.

contexts: a documentation, knowledge-base, prompt, or agent-profile reference is renamed, retired, or migrated
semantic search says the new page exists but old references may remain
hooks, validators, templates, CI text, and agent startup files consume the reference literally

trigger_signals.description: A migration changes a public or agent-facing slug, phrase, or file path.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Run deterministic old-reference searches across active operating surfaces.

trigger_signals.description: Search hits include both live configuration and historical/audit files.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Classify each hit before editing; live residue and history have different handling.

trigger_signals.description: The closeout relies on semantic search or page lookup rather than exact old-token sweep.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Exact strings can remain in hooks and prompts even when semantic lookup succeeds.

negative_signals.description: The old token is intentionally retained as historical evidence in an archive or changelog.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Do not rewrite history unless the record is an active instruction surface.

negative_signals.description: The reference is external or user-authored material outside the migration scope.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Record but do not silently edit third-party or user-controlled text.

common_wrong_assumptions: If the new page resolves, all old references are gone.
Semantic search is enough to find literal hook or prompt dependencies.
Every stale hit should be rewritten, including audit history.

first_checks.check: Search exact old slugs, paths, and trigger phrases with a deterministic text search.
first_checks.why: Literal consumers may not be discoverable by semantic search.

first_checks.check: Classify hits as live instruction/config, generated output, archive/history, or external/user material.
first_checks.why: Each class has a different safe action.

first_checks.check: Re-run the exact search after edits and preserve a summary of intentional historical hits.
first_checks.why: This proves active residue is gone without erasing provenance.

decision_rules.condition: A stale token remains in live hooks, validators, agent profiles, prompts, or CI text.
decision_rules.then: Replace it with the new canonical reference and rerun the exact sweep.

decision_rules.condition: A stale token remains only in historical audit material.
decision_rules.then: Leave it in place and record that it is historical, not an active consumer.

decision_rules.condition: A stale token appears in generated output.
decision_rules.then: Update the source generator or regenerate rather than hand-editing generated files.

do_not: Do not rely on semantic search alone for migration closeout.
Do not rewrite historical evidence just to make grep empty.
Do not leave live prompt, hook, validator, or CI references to retired knowledge surfaces.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Run an exact old-token sweep, classify every hit as live or historical, update only active consumers, then rerun the sweep.

title: Prefer structured JSON before DOM rows for SPA extraction
summary: After authorized observation of an authenticated SPA, content-filtered same-origin JSON payloads are often a safer extraction source than brittle DOM rows; keep per-item source telemetry and an explicit DOM fallback.
ai_value: Helps agents build extraction tools that are stable, observable, and auth-safe without overfitting to transient DOM or opaque endpoint names.

contexts: an authenticated SPA renders identifiers or records from same-origin JSON payloads
DOM rows are virtualized, translated, reordered, or incomplete
the extraction must remain within an already authorized observation session

trigger_signals.description: DOM selectors can find visible rows but miss stable identifiers, hidden fields, or pagination state.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Inspect captured same-origin JSON payload shapes before committing to DOM scraping.

trigger_signals.description: Endpoint names are opaque, unstable, or shared by multiple payload types.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Filter by content shape and required fields, not just URL substrings.

trigger_signals.description: Extracted items lack source-field or missing-reason telemetry.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Add per-item telemetry so extraction drift becomes visible.

negative_signals.description: Using network payloads would require bypassing authentication or accessing data outside the authorized UI session.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Do not broaden access; stay within the authorized observation boundary.

negative_signals.description: The DOM is the contractual source and JSON payloads are intentionally incomplete or unstable.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then DOM extraction with stronger assertions may be the safer contract.

common_wrong_assumptions: The visible DOM is always the safest extraction source.
Endpoint URL names are reliable enough filters for SPA payloads.
Missing identifiers can be silently skipped if most rows extract.

first_checks.check: Capture authorized same-origin JSON payloads and identify content-shape predicates for the needed records.
first_checks.why: Content shape is often more stable than endpoint names or DOM layout.

first_checks.check: Add parser tests for primary payload, fallback payload, missing identifier, and DOM fallback cases.
first_checks.why: Tests keep extraction failures observable as the SPA evolves.

first_checks.check: Emit per-item source-field and missing-reason telemetry.
first_checks.why: Telemetry distinguishes no data from extraction drift.

decision_rules.condition: Authorized structured payloads contain the needed identifiers and fields.
decision_rules.then: Use content-shape predicates to parse JSON before falling back to DOM rows.

decision_rules.condition: Structured payloads are absent or outside the authorized session.
decision_rules.then: Use the DOM path and record the absence reason rather than bypassing authentication.

decision_rules.condition: Telemetry shows missing identifiers or fallback spikes.
decision_rules.then: Inspect payload shape and DOM changes before trusting partial results.

do_not: Do not bypass authentication or broaden data access to obtain JSON.
Do not filter only by opaque endpoint names when content shape is available.
Do not silently drop items with missing identifiers.
Do not apply extraction guidance to browser mutations; cross-check admin-form-writers-need-warmup-and-readback when the task writes remote admin state.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: In an authorized SPA session, inspect same-origin JSON payload shapes, add parser/fallback tests, and emit per-item source telemetry.

title: Long-running job supervisors should safe-halt on failure spikes
summary: A supervisor that restarts every failed long-running job can turn a transient network, provider, or database outage into an infinite retry storm unless it detects rapid failure growth and stops for attention.
ai_value: When agents build keepalive loops, they should specify both the restart condition and the stop condition, including evidence that future operators can use to decide whether to resume.

contexts: imports, backfills, scrapers, sync jobs, report generation, and external API workers
jobs use tunnels, provider APIs, browser sessions, or remote databases that can fail independently of job logic
operator wants unattended progress but not uncontrolled mutation or retries

trigger_signals.description: Many failures share the same transport or connection class within a short window.
trigger_signals.pattern: ECONNREFUSED|connection closed|timeout|rate limit|5xx|failed count increased rapidly
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Prefer safe halt and handoff over blind restart.

trigger_signals.description: The supervisor has a restart loop but no failure threshold, backoff cap, or stop reason artifact.
trigger_signals.pattern: while true|restart always|nohup loop|no threshold|no halt condition
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Add a stop condition before relying on unattended execution.

negative_signals.description: The job is read-only, externally idempotent, cheap, and already has exponential backoff plus alerting.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Automatic retries may be acceptable when blast radius and cost are bounded.

negative_signals.description: A human explicitly authorized an emergency retry loop with a time/cost bound and monitoring owner.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Some operational incidents require aggressive retries, but only with explicit bounds.

common_wrong_assumptions: Unattended means always restart.
A retry loop is safer than stopping because it needs less human attention.
Connection failures are harmless if the write path is idempotent.

first_checks.check: Define maximum consecutive failures, maximum failure rate, backoff behavior, and the artifact written when the supervisor stops.
first_checks.why: Future agents need to know whether the stop was intentional protection or a crash.

first_checks.check: After a safe halt, inspect the latest failure classes before resuming instead of only checking whether the process is dead.
first_checks.why: The process may have stopped because the guard worked as designed.

decision_rules.condition: Failures spike in a way consistent with transport/provider outage rather than isolated item-level errors.
decision_rules.then: Stop the loop, write counts and failure classes, and require a deliberate resume after diagnosis.

do_not: Do not implement Restart=always or while-true loops without a failure-spike stop condition for mutable long-running jobs.
Do not treat a guarded safe halt as an incident by itself; inspect the stop reason first.
Do not publish private service names, tunnel targets, account IDs, URLs, or organization-specific queue names in public lessons.

Do not confuse failure-spike safe halts with production-incident-safe-halt-scope-boundary; cross-check that record when the stop reason is an irreversible or approval boundary rather than retry-storm protection.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When creating or reviewing a supervisor, require both restart criteria and safe-halt criteria with a durable stop summary.

risk.notes: Candidate generalizes one private supervised import halt; thresholds and retry policy must be adapted to each system's cost and mutation risk.

title: Tenant RLS can hide resumable jobs from no-tenant schedulers
summary: A global or no-tenant scheduler can conclude no resumable job exists when row-level security hides tenant-scoped running rows without throwing an authorization error.
ai_value: Helps agents debug zero-row scheduler discovery results by comparing tenant-scoped diagnostics and moving expired-lease discovery inside tenant context.

contexts: auto-resume, watchdog, or scheduler flows inspect tenant-scoped background jobs under row-level security
expired leases or heartbeats should be resumed
global discovery runs outside tenant context

trigger_signals.description: A job remains running while its lease or heartbeat is expired.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The resume candidate may exist even if the global query cannot see it.

trigger_signals.description: A global watchdog reports no running job or no resume candidate, but tenant-scoped diagnostics can see the stuck run.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Compare scoped and no-tenant visibility before restarting processes.

trigger_signals.description: The no-tenant query returns zero rows without an authorization error.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: RLS can hide rows silently; absence is not proof of completion.

trigger_signals.description: Restarting web or worker processes does not resume the job.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The discovery query remains outside the required tenant context.

negative_signals.description: There is truly no active tenant, the job completed, the lease is still fresh, or the candidate tenant list intentionally excludes a disabled tenant.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Verify scoped read-only status and lease timestamps before changing resume behavior.

negative_signals.description: The scheduler is designed to use a privileged, audited cross-tenant read that bypasses RLS and the query evidence proves it returned a complete set.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then the zero rows likely have another cause.

common_wrong_assumptions: A zero-row scheduler query means no resumable job exists.
A process restart fixes resume discovery.
Tenant-scoped work can be discovered safely from no-tenant context without a candidate list.

first_checks.check: Use a narrow safe tenant-candidate source, then enter tenant context before querying expired leases or resumable runs.
first_checks.why: Discovery itself is tenant-scoped work under RLS.

first_checks.check: Keep the one-writer lease check inside the tenant-scoped transaction before launching work.
first_checks.why: Visibility repair must not create duplicate workers.

first_checks.check: Test a fallback path where the primary tenant list is empty or RLS-hidden, then assert each candidate is queried under tenant context.
first_checks.why: The fixture captures the silent-zero-row discriminator.

first_checks.check: Use read-only incident evidence: run status, lease expiry, scheduler result, and scoped diagnostic visibility.
first_checks.why: Production rescue needs narrow evidence and gates.

decision_rules.condition: No-tenant discovery returns zero rows but scoped diagnostics show expired running work.
decision_rules.then: Iterate a narrow safe tenant-candidate list, enter tenant context per candidate, query expired leases, and re-check the lease inside the transaction before launch.

decision_rules.condition: Scoped diagnostics also show no expired work or the lease is still valid.
decision_rules.then: Do not apply the RLS-hidden resume fix; investigate scheduler timing or job completion instead.

do_not: Do not broad-enumerate tenants or credentials to solve visibility.
Do not launch work outside the tenant-scoped lease transaction.
Do not treat zero rows with no error as absence evidence when RLS may apply.

Do not include private service names, internal URLs, account identifiers, incident identifiers, private repository paths, tenant/store names, setup-card field names, low-level endpoint strings or organization-specific tooling in public lessons.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Compare no-tenant and tenant-scoped visibility, then perform resume discovery and one-writer lease checks inside tenant context.

title: Terminal-state recovery flags must cover downstream mutations
summary: A recovery flag that bypasses only the first terminal-state guard can still fail or mutate later layers unexpectedly. Recovery semantics must cover every downstream mutation path intentionally.
ai_value: Helps agents design repair modes that are auditable, side-effect-bounded, and not merely a narrow parser bypass.

contexts: a wrapper or tool has terminal records that normally cannot be reopened
a repair mode adds an allow flag for skipped, completed, retired, or failed states
downstream setup, expensive initialization, or mutation happens after the first guard

trigger_signals.description: A flag name says allow or recover, but only the first validation branch checks it.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Audit every later mutation path before trusting the recovery mode.

trigger_signals.description: The tool performs expensive setup before discovering the terminal-state repair is not actually allowed.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Move terminal validation ahead of setup or split preflight from repair.

trigger_signals.description: A repair command can silently reopen, reactivate, or rewrite a terminal record.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Require an explicit repair-only action and evidence, not a normal active-state transition.

negative_signals.description: The recovery mode is side-effect-free and only reports the repair plan.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A diagnostic preflight may safely inspect terminal records without full mutation semantics.

negative_signals.description: All downstream mutations are explicitly covered by tests for terminal input.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then the flag may already have the intended end-to-end semantics.

common_wrong_assumptions: One allow flag at the parser layer changes the meaning of the whole workflow.
Raw mutation is acceptable when the safe wrapper cannot repair terminal state.
If the first guard passes, later setup and mutation cannot violate terminal semantics.

first_checks.check: Inject a terminal record and run the recovery path in dry-run or test mode.
first_checks.why: The test proves whether downstream code still assumes active state.

first_checks.check: Assert that no active-state transition APIs are called during repair.
first_checks.why: Recovery should repair the intended artifact, not silently reopen it.

first_checks.check: Place terminal-state validation before expensive or irreversible setup.
first_checks.why: Rejected recovery should fail before costly side effects.

decision_rules.condition: A recovery flag affects only an early guard.
decision_rules.then: Make every downstream mutation either repair-aware or explicitly refused before setup.

decision_rules.condition: A terminal record needs narrow artifact repair.
decision_rules.then: Provide a scoped repair command with evidence rather than normalizing direct data edits.

decision_rules.condition: The requested recovery would reopen or alter terminal truth.
decision_rules.then: Stop and route through the appropriate gate for state-changing recovery.

do_not: Do not let allow flags become partial parser bypasses.
Do not perform expensive setup before deciding whether terminal recovery is allowed.
Do not normalize raw mutation because the wrapper lacks a repair mode.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Test recovery against terminal fixtures and verify every downstream mutation path is intentionally repair-aware or refused.

title: Webhook acknowledgements and auth identity must follow the provider contract literally
summary: Webhook receivers can fail by treating transport success, structured provider result codes, persistence timing, and authentication identity as one layer. Model each contract layer explicitly.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid hiding actionable provider result codes, acknowledging before durable persistence, or trusting display identifiers as authentication truth.

contexts: a webhook provider expects HTTP 200 plus a structured result body for receiver-known failures
the receiver must authenticate a request using secrets, signatures, or source identity
external notifications are acknowledged before local durable state is written

trigger_signals.description: The provider documentation distinguishes HTTP acknowledgement from an application-level result code.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Return the transport status the provider expects and put actionable receiver-known errors in the structured body.

trigger_signals.description: The handler uses a public display identifier, URL slug, or request label as authentication truth.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Fail closed until the provider contract says that identifier is security-relevant and verifies it cryptographically or through a trusted channel.

trigger_signals.description: The handler returns success to the provider before the local side effect is durably persisted.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Move acknowledgement after durable persistence or make retry/reconciliation semantics explicit.

negative_signals.description: The provider explicitly requires non-2xx transport failures for the exact condition.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then the structured-body pattern may be wrong; follow the documented retry contract.

negative_signals.description: The identifier is a signed claim or verified subject in the provider contract.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then it can contribute to auth, but only after signature and freshness checks.

common_wrong_assumptions: HTTP 200 always means the webhook operation succeeded semantically.
A 4xx response is the clearest way to communicate every receiver-known error.
A public account or object identifier in the payload is enough to authenticate the sender.

first_checks.check: Read the provider contract for transport acknowledgement, structured result body, retry behavior, and auth identity separately.
first_checks.why: Webhook contracts often split these layers in non-obvious ways.

first_checks.check: Log safe diagnostics such as hash prefix and payload length rather than raw secret or payload values.
first_checks.why: Diagnostics should prove parsing/auth paths without leaking credentials or private content.

first_checks.check: Test the known-error path and the durable-persist-before-ack path.
first_checks.why: Both paths often pass happy-path smoke while still failing real provider retries.

decision_rules.condition: The provider expects HTTP 200 with a structured result code for receiver-known errors.
decision_rules.then: Return the documented transport acknowledgement and encode the actionable error in the structured response body.

decision_rules.condition: Auth truth is ambiguous or based only on public identifiers.
decision_rules.then: Reject or quarantine the request until the authenticated identity source is verified against the contract.

decision_rules.condition: The external sender may retry based on acknowledgement timing.
decision_rules.then: Persist the local side effect before acknowledging, or document a retry-safe reconciliation path.

do_not: Do not collapse HTTP status, application result code, persistence, and authentication identity into one boolean success flag.
Do not expose raw secrets or payloads in diagnostics.
Do not accept a public display identifier as authorization proof by default.

title: When a webhook uses an HMAC-over-raw-body signature, verify the raw bytes before parsing
summary: When an inbound webhook authenticates senders with an HMAC/shared-secret signature computed over the raw request body, an agent that calls request.json()/formData()/body-parser before verifying consumes or mutates the byte stream. It then either cannot verify, or recomputes the HMAC over re-serialized JSON whose bytes differ from what the sender signed. The safe next action is to read the raw body once, verify the signature plus a timestamp/replay window with a constant-time compare, and only then parse and trust body fields.
ai_value: Stops agents from shipping webhook endpoints that silently accept forged or replayed deliveries, fail verification against the real signing string, leak the digest through a non-constant-time compare, or act on tenant/account fields from an unverified body. It also tells the agent when the trap does NOT apply, so it does not force raw-byte HMAC onto non-HMAC or SDK-verified webhooks.

contexts: implementing an inbound HTTP webhook or callback endpoint that authenticates senders via an HMAC or shared-secret signature header over the request body
a web framework or middleware parses the request body (JSON, form, multipart) or runs schema validation before the route handler
the provider documents a signing string over the raw bytes plus a timestamp or nonce (for example {timestamp}.{body} or v0:{timestamp}:{body})
the request body carries tenant, account, user, or integration identifiers that the handler will act on
adapting a provider-neutral webhook template before a specific provider's signature contract is finalized

trigger_signals.description: The body is parsed (json(), formData(), express.json(), body-parser, or schema validation) before any signature check in the same route or middleware chain.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The raw byte stream is consumed or normalized before verification, so verification will be impossible or run over the wrong bytes. Reorder to verify first.

trigger_signals.description: The HMAC input is built from re-serialized parsed data instead of the exact received bytes.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Re-serialization changes whitespace, key order, or encoding, so the signed bytes differ from JSON.stringify(parsed). Verification is invalid even if a self-signed test passes.

trigger_signals.description: A tenant, account, user, or integration identifier is read from the body, query, or header before verification succeeds.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Attacker-controlled fields are driving authorization or data writes before authentication. Parse and trust fields only after verification.

trigger_signals.description: The signature covers only the body; there is no timestamp, nonce, or delivery-id binding and no freshness window check.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The endpoint is replayable: a captured valid delivery can be resent indefinitely. Bind and check a timestamp/nonce.

trigger_signals.description: The signature is compared with ==, ===, or string equality on the digest.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Byte-by-byte short-circuit comparison leaks the digest through timing. Use a constant-time compare after length and format checks.

trigger_signals.description: Tests sign one happy-path fixture only; there are no malformed, missing-header, stale-timestamp, or replay assertions.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The security-relevant paths are the negative ones and are unverified. Add negative-path tests before trusting the endpoint.

negative_signals.description: A maintained provider SDK or framework binding already captures the raw body and verifies the signature before the handler runs (for example a construct-event helper).
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The raw-body-before-parse obligation is already met upstream. Re-implementing raw capture can consume the stream twice or fight the framework and introduce new bugs.

negative_signals.description: The provider's documented signature scheme is computed over a canonicalized or constructed representation of selected fields, not the literal received bytes (for example a signed string-to-sign or a SHA256 over a constructed message; AWS SNS is one such scheme).
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Raw-byte verification would wrongly fail. Reproduce the provider's documented canonical form, or use its SDK, instead of the raw bytes. Raw-body-before-parse is not provider-universal.

negative_signals.description: The endpoint's authentication is transport- or token-based: mutual TLS, an asymmetric/public-key-verified JWT/JWS, or an IP allow-list on a trusted internal-only network, with no shared-secret body HMAC.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: There is no body-HMAC signing string to verify; the trap is out of scope and different verification rules apply.

negative_signals.description: No shared secret or signing scheme exists between sender and receiver (for example an unsigned internal event bus protected by separate access control).
negative_signals.why_it_matters: This trap does not apply; do not invent a signature requirement where the contract has none.

negative_signals.description: The handler is read-only/idempotent and takes no privileged action or data write from body fields.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The forgery/replay harm model (acting on unverified fields) is bounded. Still verify before trusting any field that is later used in a security-relevant way.

common_wrong_assumptions: I can parse the JSON first and then verify the signature over the parsed object.
Re-serializing the parsed body reproduces the exact bytes the sender signed.
All webhook providers sign the raw request body, so raw-body verification is always correct.
The HMAC is over just the body, so I do not need the timestamp.
Idempotency or delivery-id dedupe is the same as replay protection.
A plain ==/=== comparison on the hex digest is fine.
A passing happy-path test means verification is correct.
Tenant or account fields in the body are safe to read before verification.

first_checks.check: Read the route handler and middleware registration top to bottom; confirm the raw body is captured and the signature plus timestamp are verified before any parse, schema validation, or service call.
first_checks.why: Ordering is the root cause: parsing first consumes or normalizes the bytes that must be verified.

first_checks.check: Confirm the provider's signature contract: is it an HMAC/shared-secret over the raw body, a canonicalized string-to-sign, or non-HMAC transport auth?
first_checks.why: The trap only applies to HMAC-over-raw-body schemes. Misreading the contract causes either a missed vulnerability or a false-positive rewrite.
files: existing verification code or SDK usage

first_checks.check: If HMAC-over-raw-body: confirm the HMAC input is the exact received bytes matched to the documented signing string, not JSON.stringify(parsed).
first_checks.why: Whitespace, key order, and encoding differences in re-serialized JSON break verification.

first_checks.check: Confirm a timestamp or nonce is bound into the signature and a bounded freshness window (commonly a few minutes) is enforced, and that comparison is constant-time after length/format checks.
first_checks.why: Without a freshness window valid deliveries are replayable; string equality on the digest leaks it via timing.

first_checks.check: Confirm tests cover bad signature, missing signature/timestamp header, stale timestamp, success, and replay, not just one happy fixture.
first_checks.why: The negative paths are the security-relevant ones and are usually the unverified gaps.

decision_rules.condition: The provider contract is an HMAC/shared-secret signature over the raw body, and the body is parsed before signature verification in the handler or middleware chain.
decision_rules.then: Capture the raw body once (size-capped), verify the signature and timestamp, then parse. In Express, register the raw/verify route before express.json() or retain the buffer via a body-parser verify hook.

decision_rules.condition: The HMAC is computed over re-serialized or parsed data instead of the received bytes.
decision_rules.then: Build the HMAC input from the exact received bytes following the provider's documented signing string (for example {timestamp}.{body} or v0:{timestamp}:{body}).

decision_rules.condition: The signature is the only signed element and there is no freshness/replay check.
decision_rules.then: Verify the timestamp is part of the signed string and reject deliveries outside a bounded window; do not rely on idempotency alone for replay protection.

decision_rules.condition: The digest is compared with ==/===/string equality.
decision_rules.then: Replace with a constant-time compare (for example crypto.timingSafeEqual, hmac.compare_digest, or secure_compare) after length and format checks.

decision_rules.condition: A provider SDK already returns a verified raw body, or the scheme signs canonicalized/constructed content, or authentication is mTLS/asymmetric/internal-trusted with no body HMAC.
decision_rules.then: This trap does not apply. Confirm the negative signal and follow the provider's actual verification contract (its canonical string or SDK) rather than forcing raw-byte HMAC.

decision_rules.condition: Tenant/account/source fields are read or acted on before verification passes.
decision_rules.then: Treat as a security-sensitive change: do not auto-apply. Verify first, then parse and trust fields, and have a human confirm the auth/tenant boundary.

do_not: Do not verify a signature over re-serialized/parsed JSON instead of the received bytes.
Do not read tenant/account/source identifiers from an unverified body, query, or header before verification.
Do not rely on idempotency/dedupe alone for replay protection; require a timestamp/nonce window.
Do not compare digests with ==/===/string equality.
Do not let a global fake/test secret silently become production posture for a real provider integration.
Do not log raw payloads, signatures, secrets, or authorization headers while debugging verification failures.
Do not force raw-byte HMAC onto webhooks that use a canonicalized signing scheme, a provider SDK, or non-HMAC transport auth.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Identify the provider's signature contract first. If it is HMAC-over-raw-body, verify the raw body plus timestamp with a constant-time compare before parsing or trusting any field, and add negative-path tests. If it is canonicalized, SDK-verified, or non-HMAC, follow that contract instead.

risk.notes: Touches authentication, authorization, and trust boundaries: a wrong change can silently accept forged or replayed webhooks or break legitimate delivery processing. The exact signing string, tolerance window, secret lookup, replay store, and response codes must follow each real provider's contract. This record guides diagnosis and verify-before-parse ordering; it does not authorize disabling verification or relaxing a window in production.

sources.excerpt: The hash signature will appear in each delivery as the value of the X-Hub-Signature-256 header. ... Never use a plain == operator. Instead consider using a method like secure_compare or crypto.timingSafeEqual, which performs a 'constant time' string comparison to help mitigate certain timing attacks against regular equality operators. ... Make sure that the payload and headers are not modified before verification.
sources.supports: Official source for the HMAC-SHA256 signature header, the explicit requirement to use a constant-time comparison rather than ==, and the rule that the payload must not be modified before verification.

sources.excerpt: Use the raw request body, without headers, before it has been deserialized from JSON or other forms. ... Concatenate the version number, the timestamp, and the request body together, using a colon (:) as a delimiter. ... The signature depends on the timestamp to protect against replay attacks. ... For best practice, use an hmac compare function instead of directly comparing the signatures for equality.
sources.supports: Second independent provider confirming raw-body-before-deserialization, a {version}:{timestamp}:{body} signing string, timestamp-bound replay protection, and constant-time hmac comparison.

sources.excerpt: To ensure message integrity and prevent spoofing, you must verify the signature before processing any Amazon SNS messages. ... SignatureVersion2 - Uses an SHA256 hash of the message. ... The AWS SDKs for Amazon SNS provide built-in validation logic, reducing the risk of misimplementation. ... Reject any message with an unexpected TopicArn to prevent spoofing.
sources.supports: Counterexample grounding the negative signal: a provider whose signature is computed over a constructed representation of the message (with SDK-provided validation), not an HMAC over the raw HTTP request body, so raw-body-before-parse is not provider-universal.

title: Hot count polling can become the data import incident
summary: Polling exact target-table counts for a live import progress display can create more database load than the import itself. Progress should come from job-owned counters, watermarks, sampled metrics, or terminal summaries unless an exact count is proven cheap.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid adding an apparently harmless progress dashboard query that turns a long-running import into a database CPU incident.

applies_to.ecosystem: agent-built data import and backfill workflows
contexts: a UI or status API refreshes every few seconds while an import is running
target tables are large, growing, heavily indexed, or receiving writes from the same job
operators ask for progress, ETA, or denominator estimates during a multi-hour or multi-day run

trigger_signals.description: The status endpoint computes progress with exact count queries against import target tables on every poll.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat the progress read path as part of the load-bearing design, not as harmless UI code.

trigger_signals.description: Database CPU rises while the import is running, and query samples show repeated aggregate scans from the status or dashboard path.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Mitigate the read-side polling before further increasing worker throttles or changing write code.

trigger_signals.description: The product only needs approximate progress or a heartbeat state, but implementation asks the database for exact live totals.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Use job-owned approximate counters or previous-run summaries instead of exact target counts.

negative_signals.description: The counted relation is tiny, static, indexed for the exact aggregate, or maintained as a cheap metadata counter in the database engine.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Exact counts can be safe when proven cheap in the target database and scale envelope.

negative_signals.description: The count is run once as an operator-gated diagnostic, not repeatedly on the user-facing hot path.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: One-off diagnostics have a different risk profile from background polling.

common_wrong_assumptions: A read-only progress query cannot be the cause of a production incident.
Exact target-table counts are the most honest way to display import progress.
Throttling the writer is enough when the status page is also querying the hot tables.
A progress UI can be designed after the import logic without affecting database load.

first_checks.check: List every query executed by the status endpoint while a run is active and mark which ones touch target tables versus job-state tables.
first_checks.why: Progress reads often look small in code but run frequently enough to dominate load.

first_checks.check: Replace live exact target counts with job-maintained counters, phase high-water marks, prior-run performance summaries, or sampled/async statistics, then compare database CPU and status correctness.
first_checks.why: The safe design keeps observability while removing hot aggregate scans.

first_checks.check: Make UI copy explicit about approximate denominators and heartbeat-derived state when exact counts are intentionally avoided.
first_checks.why: Operators need honest semantics without paying for exact live counts.

decision_rules.condition: A live import status path repeatedly runs exact aggregate counts over the target tables and approximate progress would satisfy the operator need.
decision_rules.then: Read heartbeat, job counters, watermarks, and prior-run summaries; forbid target-table count polling on the hot status path.

do_not: Do not add repeated exact count(*) polling to a live import dashboard without measuring the real query plan and refresh cadence at production scale.
Do not claim the import writer is the only load source until the progress/status read path has been profiled.
Do not hide approximate semantics; label estimated denominators and ETA clearly.
Do not publish private provider names, tenant identifiers, database names, internal URLs, account IDs, or repository paths in public lessons.

Do not treat this as only generic bounded polling; cross-check agent-hosts-need-bounded-polling for host polling cadence and cartesian-distinct-counts-can-dos-a-production-db/page-before-expensive-aggregation for query-shape count traps.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When asked for live import progress, design the status path from job-owned state first and treat exact target-table counts as an operator-gated diagnostic unless proven cheap.

risk.notes: Candidate is based on one private production-backed import incident; promotion needs independent review and de-identification.

sources.supports: A long-running import's progress page polled exact target-table counts every few seconds while writes were active. Removing those counts and using job-owned counters/performance summaries was part of reducing database CPU to a stable range.

title: Idempotent reruns can replace separate resume state in imports
summary: When an import can cheaply detect already-committed records and upsert batches idempotently, a separate resume button or state machine may add more operational risk than value.
ai_value: Before adding resume/cancel/status complexity to a failed import, agents should ask whether rerunning the same operation with no-op skip and idempotent writes safely provides the resume behavior.

contexts: large imports or backfills where failures are common and partial commits are expected
records have stable external IDs, watermarks, hashes, or other keys that allow duplicate detection
the operator UI is becoming more complex to represent stop/resume states

trigger_signals.description: The proposed UI or API adds explicit resume state, but the write path already has stable identifiers and can detect unchanged rows.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Evaluate idempotent rerun before expanding the state machine.

trigger_signals.description: A rerun after partial completion mostly skips already-written work and quickly reaches the missing tail.
trigger_signals.pattern: attempted high|inserted low|updated low|no-op skip|already committed
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The operation may already be resume-by-reexecution.

negative_signals.description: The external source is non-deterministic, destructive, or charges per read in a way that makes reruns materially harmful.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A dedicated checkpoint/resume mechanism may be necessary when re-reading is unsafe or costly.

negative_signals.description: The write path lacks stable uniqueness keys or cannot distinguish duplicate from changed records.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Rerun-as-resume depends on reliable idempotency boundaries.

common_wrong_assumptions: A failed long-running import always needs a separate resume button.
More explicit state always improves operator safety.
No-op detection is only an optimization, not a simplification of the recovery model.

first_checks.check: Identify the idempotency key for each imported entity and prove duplicate writes are skipped or converted into safe upserts.
first_checks.why: Without stable keys, rerun-as-resume can duplicate or corrupt data.

first_checks.check: Run a bounded partial import, then rerun the same range and compare attempted/inserted/updated/no-op counts.
first_checks.why: This demonstrates whether already-committed work is safely skipped and whether the tail progresses.

decision_rules.condition: Rerun performs safe no-op skip/upsert for already-committed records and reaches missing records without manual state repair.
decision_rules.then: Prefer one run button plus clear progress/history over a separate resume state machine.

do_not: Do not remove resume controls until idempotency is proven with a bounded partial-run test.
Do not use this pattern for destructive imports or external APIs where re-reading has material cost without a human gate.
Do not publish private provider names, tenant identifiers, URLs, account IDs, or internal repository paths in public lessons.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When asked to add resume logic, first test whether idempotent rerun with no-op skip already gives a simpler and safer recovery model.

risk.notes: Candidate is based on one private production-backed import redesign and needs review before promotion.

sources.supports: A long-running import was simplified by batch upserts plus no-op skip; rerunning became the resume path, and a rollback/repair probe confirmed recovery behavior.

title: Inventory imports need target reconciliation before apply
summary: Inventory or stock imports must prove final target master-data projection and reconciliation totals before apply. Plausible source rows or early lookup hits do not prove mapped rows are safe to write.
ai_value: Helps agents stop zero-mapped or misprojected imports before they mutate inventory and route missing master-data projection as a prerequisite.

contexts: an import maps source stock, inventory, or lot rows onto internal master-data targets
early identifier lookups succeed but final target rows may still be zero
the task is to apply quantities, not silently create master entities

trigger_signals.description: Source rows and totals look plausible, but the final target projection maps zero rows.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Stop before apply and repair master-data projection first.

trigger_signals.description: Checks verify nearby lookup tables rather than the exact foreign-key target used by the apply.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Probe the final target table and join used by the write path.

trigger_signals.description: The import code is tempted to create missing master entities while applying quantities.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Separate master-data creation from stock apply unless explicitly authorized.

trigger_signals.description: Reconciliation compares source totals only, not mapped/applied/skipped totals.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Add totals at each projection boundary.

negative_signals.description: The apply path intentionally includes reviewed master-data creation with separate validation and gates.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then creation is in scope, but it still needs its own reconciliation evidence.

negative_signals.description: The source rows are zero after explicit filters and that is the expected business state.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Zero mapped rows is not always an error when source zero is expected and proven.

common_wrong_assumptions: If source rows are non-zero, the target mapping must be non-zero.
Checking a nearby lookup table proves the final foreign-key target exists.
Inventory apply can create missing master data as a convenience.

first_checks.check: Dry-run the final target projection used by the apply path and count mapped, skipped, and unmapped rows.
first_checks.why: The final projection, not early lookups, determines whether writes are valid.

first_checks.check: Compare source totals, mapped totals, skipped reasons, and would-apply totals before mutation.
first_checks.why: Reconciliation at each boundary catches zero-mapped and partial projection failures.

first_checks.check: Fail closed when mapped rows are zero but source rows are non-zero.
first_checks.why: This is usually a missing projection prerequisite, not a successful no-op.

decision_rules.condition: Source rows are non-zero and final mapped rows are zero.
decision_rules.then: Do not apply inventory changes; route the missing target projection as a separate prerequisite.

decision_rules.condition: Some rows map and some do not.
decision_rules.then: Apply only if skip reasons and totals match the authorized scope.

decision_rules.condition: The import would create master data while applying inventory.
decision_rules.then: Separate and authorize master-data creation before quantity mutation.

do_not: Do not treat plausible source counts as target mapping proof.
Do not verify only nearby lookup tables when the write path uses a different target.
Do not silently create master entities inside an inventory apply task.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Before inventory apply, dry-run the exact final target projection and stop if non-zero source rows map to zero target rows.
