title: Long-running HTTP handlers are fragile batch runners
summary: A large import or backfill should not depend on one HTTP request staying open through a load balancer or proxy. Use a resident worker or short start request plus durable progress and idempotent resume behavior.
ai_value: When an agent is asked to run or build a long import, this record should make it check transport timeouts before treating a 504/timeout as only an application bug.

contexts: imports or backfills expected to run longer than common gateway, proxy, or platform request limits
operator UI triggers a job by POST and waits for the full result
progress, ETA, or resumability is needed after the initiating browser or HTTP client disconnects

trigger_signals.description: The requested implementation runs the whole import inside one API route, controller, function, or web request.
trigger_signals.pattern: POST /import|route handler|controller|server action|wait for completion|long request|504|gateway timeout
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Design a job handoff instead of stretching the HTTP timeout.

trigger_signals.description: The operation has chunking, ETA, progress rows, or resume requirements.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The user-facing request should start or observe the job, not be the job owner.

negative_signals.description: The entire operation is proven to finish comfortably below every relevant platform timeout and has no need to continue after disconnect.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A simple synchronous request can be correct for genuinely small bounded work.

negative_signals.description: The platform provides a first-class long-running job primitive behind the same API surface.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The architectural issue is not HTTP syntax itself but tying job lifetime to a client request.

common_wrong_assumptions: Increasing the HTTP timeout is enough to make a long import reliable.
A gateway timeout means the server-side work failed.
Chunking inside a request is equivalent to a durable worker.
Progress UI can be added later without first deciding where job state lives.

first_checks.check: List every request timeout between the browser/client and the handler: client, framework, proxy, load balancer, platform, and database driver.
first_checks.why: The smallest timeout sets the real synchronous budget.

first_checks.check: Prove job state survives HTTP disconnect by starting a bounded run, disconnecting or exceeding the former timeout, and reading progress from a durable source.
first_checks.why: This distinguishes a worker design from a merely longer request.
files: staging or reviewed production test plan

decision_rules.condition: The expected runtime can exceed a gateway/proxy/client timeout or must keep running after the operator page closes.
decision_rules.then: Make HTTP start/status endpoints short and bounded; run the import in a resident worker, queue consumer, scheduler, or platform job with idempotent resume/retry semantics.

do_not: Do not stretch only one timeout without checking upstream and downstream limits.
Do not treat a timed-out client request as proof that the background work stopped; verify runtime state separately.
Do not publish private URLs, tenant identifiers, account IDs, database names, or internal repository paths in public lessons.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When a batch API may run long, design the HTTP surface as start/status/control and put job ownership in a worker with durable progress.

risk.notes: Candidate is based on a private production-backed import redesign; promotion needs review and de-identification.

sources.supports: A production import initially hit the web request boundary; it became reliable after moving execution to a resident runner with durable progress and short HTTP control/status calls.

title: Import progress state must match cursor semantics
summary: If two import modes interpret a cursor differently, they must not share the same progress row or aggregate run key. The state key must include every dimension that changes resume, watermark, window, or counter semantics.
ai_value: Before adding or reusing progress tables for full, differential, archive, retry, or per-window imports, agents should check whether the persisted key matches the meaning of the cursor and counters.

applies_to.ecosystem: agent-built data import and backfill workflows
contexts: one system supports both full backfills and incremental or differential imports
progress rows, run rows, or cursor rows are keyed by a small subset such as tenant and source
operators can start another import mode while a long-running backfill is paused, running, or resumable
a status UI displays processed counts, estimates, cursors, watermarks, or import windows

tools.name: general relational database and job-state store

trigger_signals.description: A progress table or run table is keyed only by source, tenant, account, or job name while code branches on mode, window, partition, archive/current source, or full-versus-incremental behavior.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The persisted key may be too coarse; check whether different modes can overwrite each other's cursor or counters.

trigger_signals.description: Starting a small incremental run makes the denominator jump to all historical records, or makes a full backfill resume from the wrong cursor.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: A mode/window mismatch may have reused the wrong progress row or lower-bound cursor.

trigger_signals.description: Processed counts reset on resume even though the operator-facing window has not changed, or counts accumulate across a new window even though the denominator changed.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Counter semantics are not explicit enough; distinguish per-attempt counters from per-window cumulative counters.

negative_signals.description: All modes intentionally share exactly the same cursor meaning, lower-bound policy, denominator, and counter semantics, and concurrent or interleaved starts are forbidden by a durable lease.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A compact key can be correct when the semantics are truly identical or the system prevents interleaving.

negative_signals.description: The progress row is purely ephemeral display state and is never used for resume, lower-bound selection, committed watermark, deduplication, or operator decisions.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Display-only state has lower corruption risk, though misleading UI can still be harmful.

negative_signals.description: The import can safely recompute progress from immutable committed records and does not persist mutable cursors or counters between attempts.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Some idempotent rerun designs avoid explicit progress state; the trap applies mainly when persisted state influences resume or visibility.

negative_signals.description: Processed-count stillness occurs during a long transaction while the transaction boundary has not committed.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Stillness inside one long transaction is not necessarily a stalled cursor; check transaction and commit boundaries before rewriting progress semantics.

common_wrong_assumptions: One source has one progress row, even if full and incremental imports use different cursor meanings.
Adding import_mode to logs is enough; it also has to be part of persisted uniqueness if it changes resume behavior.
A cursor can serve both as an in-flight deep position and as the committed lower bound for future incremental work.
Processed count is self-explanatory; operators will know whether it means this attempt, this window, or all history.

first_checks.check: List every field that changes import semantics: mode, source family, account or tenant, partition, window start/end, committed watermark, in-flight cursor, archive/current source, and retry attempt. Compare that list with the unique key of progress and aggregate-run state.
first_checks.why: Any missing semantic dimension can let one run overwrite another run's resume state or displayed progress.

first_checks.check: Run a bounded full-or-large window, then start a bounded incremental-or-small window, and verify that each mode's cursor, denominator, and processed count remain isolated.
first_checks.why: The failure often appears only when modes are interleaved, not when each mode is tested alone.
files: staging or reviewed production test plan

first_checks.check: Define counter labels before UI work: per-attempt processed, per-window cumulative processed, all-time imported total, estimated window total, and committed watermark should not share ambiguous names.
first_checks.why: Clear names prevent a resumed run from looking like it lost work or silently expanded scope.

decision_rules.condition: Two import modes can run or resume against the same source but use different lower bounds, cursor formats, source tables, archive/current scopes, or denominators.
decision_rules.then: Add the differentiating dimensions to the persisted progress/run key and migrate existing state forward-only; keep committed watermarks separate from in-flight cursors.

decision_rules.condition: The operator-facing import window is unchanged and a run is resumed after a partial attempt.
decision_rules.then: Continue the per-window processed counter instead of resetting it; reset only when a new window begins, or expose per-attempt and per-window counters separately.

do_not: Do not reuse one progress row for full and incremental imports merely because they target the same destination table.
Do not let a partial or failed run's in-flight cursor become the committed watermark without reconciliation.
Do not fix an inflated denominator only in UI formatting if the underlying state key still allows cursor clobbering.
Do not publish private tenant identifiers, source names, database names, URLs, account IDs, repository paths, or customer data in public lessons.
Do not classify processed-count stillness during one long transaction as a stall until transaction and commit boundaries are checked.
Do not use cursor-key fixes as proof that side effects committed; cross-check watermarks-need-committed-side-effect-evidence for completion-boundary truth.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When diagnosing import progress or resume bugs, compare cursor semantics to the persisted progress key before changing batch size, retry policy, or UI copy.

risk.notes: Candidate is based on a private production-backed import repair. Promotion needs independent review, especially around migration and live-data handling.

sources.supports: A long-running backfill and a small differential import shared progress state keyed too broadly. Starting the small mode overwrote the large mode's cursor and made estimates look like an all-history sweep. The repair separated state by mode/window, used committed watermarks for incremental lower bounds, and preserved cumulative window counters across resume.

title: Schema support for secret-like import fields is not enough; prove write-path encryption and log redaction before enabling ingestion
summary: When an import feature receives fields that behave like passwords, invite tokens, private customer gates, or other secret-like values, adding a destination column or UI checkbox does not make ingestion safe. Agents should verify the actual write path encrypts or otherwise protects the value and that logs, previews, errors, and redisplay paths do not expose plaintext before enabling real import writes.
ai_value: Prevents agents from declaring an import field implemented just because storage shape exists, while missing plaintext logging, preview, or redisplay exposure in the operational write path.

contexts: ETL or product import pipelines that map external payload fields into an internal database
Admin UIs that let users select optional import fields
Fields whose names or semantics resemble password, access code, token, secret, invite, private link, gated sale, or customer-specific purchase restriction

trigger_signals.description: A migration or model adds a destination for a secret-like field, but the code path that writes imported rows has not been audited for encryption/redaction.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat storage-shape completion as incomplete until write-path and logging behavior are verified.

trigger_signals.description: The UI can select the field for import while previews, dry-run output, debug logs, failed-row logs, or audit entries may include raw payload values.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Search display/log/error paths before enabling writes or showing the field in selectable import controls.

negative_signals.description: The field is non-sensitive public catalog data and has no credential, access-control, private-customer, or abuse-enabling meaning.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Ordinary public attributes do not need secret-handling gates, though normal data validation still applies.

negative_signals.description: The system already has tests proving encryption at rest plus redaction in logs, previews, errors, and redisplay for this exact field family.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Existing field-family coverage can be reused if the new field follows the same path and tests name the new mapping.

common_wrong_assumptions: A column named for encrypted storage means the import service already encrypts values before insert or update.
Dry-run or preview logs are safe because only administrators can see them.
Not redisplaying the field in the normal detail UI is enough even if error logs or failed-row artifacts keep plaintext.
Optional field selection is harmless until users import at scale.

first_checks.check: Trace the selected field from payload parsing through validation, preview/dry-run, write, update, error handling, and audit logging.
first_checks.why: Secret-like values often leak outside the final database column.

first_checks.check: Search for raw payload serialization around the import path and failed-row logging.
first_checks.why: Generic debug dumps can bypass field-specific redaction.

first_checks.check: Add or run tests that assert encrypted/protected storage and redacted display/log/error output for a sentinel value.
first_checks.why: A sentinel makes plaintext leaks easy to detect across artifacts.

decision_rules.condition: Only schema/UI support exists; write-path encryption or log redaction is unproven.
decision_rules.then: Record the field as prepared but not operational, keep real import writes disabled for that field, and create follow-up work for encryption/redaction tests.

decision_rules.condition: The field is actually imported and can affect customer access, credential-like behavior, or private purchase gates.
decision_rules.then: Review write, update, preview, redisplay, audit, and failure paths before production import use.

do_not: Do not mark a secret-like import field complete solely because a database column or mapping row exists.
Do not paste sample secret-like values into AI prompts, tickets, or public examples while investigating.
Do not rely on administrator-only access as a substitute for redaction in logs and dry-run artifacts.
Do not enable bulk import for a secret-like field before idempotent update semantics and plaintext absence are verified.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: If a secret-like field appears in an import mapping, classify the current state as storage-prepared vs write-path-safe, then verify encryption/redaction with a sentinel test before enabling real import writes.

risk.notes: This trap touches confidentiality and access-boundary behavior. It does not authorize changing auth, permissions, production data, or logging retention without the applicable human/reviewed gate.

sources.supports: A product-import handoff distinguished an encryption column being prepared from the later, separate task of safely writing a restricted-access field with plaintext logging prohibited.

title: Timeout fixes must be applied at the effective layer
summary: Changing a timeout option in the nearest request call may not affect the actual deadline. Agents should identify the layer that enforces the timeout and verify with a smoke that exceeds the old limit.
ai_value: Prevents agents from repeatedly patching timeout literals that look plausible but are ignored by the driver, pool, proxy, or platform actually enforcing the deadline.

contexts: database or provider reads fail at a consistent deadline despite local timeout changes
client libraries have both per-request and connection/pool/global timeout options
a query or API call is expected to be slow but safe when bounded by chunking and cancellation rules

trigger_signals.description: Failures still happen at the same fixed duration after a timeout option was changed nearby.
trigger_signals.pattern: timeout after 15s|timeout after 30s|same deadline|requestTimeout|pool timeout|connection timeout
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The changed option is probably not the enforcing layer.

trigger_signals.description: The client has multiple timeout scopes such as request, pool, connection, statement, socket, proxy, or load balancer.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Map the timeout hierarchy before changing code.

negative_signals.description: The failure duration changes exactly as expected after the local option change and is covered by a regression test or timed smoke.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The effective layer may already have been identified.

negative_signals.description: The slow operation should be optimized or indexed rather than allowed to run longer.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Timeout extension can hide an algorithmic or data-model problem.

common_wrong_assumptions: The timeout option closest to the query is always the one being enforced.
A code diff that increases a timeout proves the runtime deadline changed.
A successful fast query validates a timeout fix.

first_checks.check: Create a timeout map naming every layer that can cancel the call and its current configured deadline.
first_checks.why: The actual deadline is the earliest active cancellation source.

first_checks.check: Run a bounded smoke that is expected to take longer than the old deadline and shorter than the new one, then record measured duration and success/failure.
first_checks.why: Only a >old-timeout smoke proves the effective deadline moved.
files: reviewed test query or API call

decision_rules.condition: A timeout remains fixed after local option changes or the client exposes pool/global timeout settings.
decision_rules.then: Change the enforcing layer, keep the operation bounded, and verify with a timed smoke that crosses the former deadline.

do_not: Do not claim a timeout fix from a fast-path smoke that completes below the old deadline.
Do not increase timeouts to mask an unbounded query, missing index, or runaway batch without a separate design check.
Do not publish private driver configs, hostnames, tenant identifiers, SQL text containing business data, or internal paths in public lessons.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When a timeout patch seems ignored, map cancellation layers and verify the selected layer with a timed smoke exceeding the former limit.

risk.notes: Candidate is based on a private production-backed import; timed smokes against live systems require normal production/data gates.

sources.supports: A database import continued to hit the old deadline until the timeout was moved from per-request code to the client pool configuration and verified with a query exceeding the former limit.

title: Import watermarks need committed side-effect evidence
summary: An import watermark or success marker should advance only from committed side effects. Audit rows and progress evidence must not become resume truth until the durable write they describe has actually succeeded.
ai_value: Helps agents distinguish in-flight progress, audit visibility, committed watermarks, and external acknowledgements when repairing imports or retries.

contexts: incremental imports maintain watermarks, cursors, audit rows, or progress tables
a partial run wrote evidence rows but failed during the downstream side effect
uniform downstream exceptions make agents suspect the upstream provider first

trigger_signals.description: A watermark advances before the destination mutation commits.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat the watermark as unsafe; separate in-flight cursor from committed lower bound.

trigger_signals.description: Evidence rows are written before the side effect they claim to prove.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Make those rows attempt/audit state only, not resume state.

trigger_signals.description: A whole batch fails with the same downstream exception class after source reads succeed.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Investigate the local side-effect path before assuming an upstream outage.

negative_signals.description: The destination operation is atomic with the watermark update in one durable transaction.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The completion boundary may already be correct, though external acknowledgements still need review.

negative_signals.description: The progress evidence is explicitly labelled attempt-only and never read by resume logic.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Attempt logs can be useful without becoming committed state.

common_wrong_assumptions: If source reads succeeded, the import can advance the watermark.
Audit rows are harmless even when resume logic later reads them as truth.
A uniform exception across the batch must mean the upstream system is down.

first_checks.check: Trace the order of source read, destination write, audit/progress write, watermark advance, and external acknowledgement.
first_checks.why: The committed side effect must be the boundary for success.

first_checks.check: Probe a failed run and verify whether its rows can influence future resume lower bounds.
first_checks.why: Failed attempts should be visible but not promoted automatically.

first_checks.check: Classify exception uniformity before retrying.
first_checks.why: Uniform local exceptions usually require code/config repair, not upstream backoff.

decision_rules.condition: A watermark, lower bound, or success marker advances before durable destination commit.
decision_rules.then: Move the state transition after the committed side effect and keep in-flight cursors separate.

decision_rules.condition: Failed attempt evidence exists but is not safe for resume.
decision_rules.then: Keep it visible for audit while excluding it from resume selection unless a reviewed repair promotes it.

decision_rules.condition: Uniform downstream exceptions appear after successful source reads.
decision_rules.then: Inspect local destination schema, permissions, serialization, and transaction boundaries before broad upstream retries.

do_not: Do not let failed-run cursors become committed watermarks by accident.
Do not acknowledge external notifications before the local persistence contract is satisfied; see webhook-ack-layer-and-auth-identity.
Do not hide partial attempts; make them audit-visible but not authoritative.
Do not use committed side-effect evidence as a substitute for persisted cursor-key design; cross-check progress-state-must-match-cursor-semantics when modes/windows can overwrite progress state.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Trace the import state transitions and ensure only committed destination effects can advance resume or watermark truth.

title: Cartesian distinct counts can DoS a production database
summary: A query that counts distinct entities after joining multiple option, dimension, or composition tables can accidentally materialize a cartesian product. Split the query into pre-aggregated CTEs or independent counts, and add an effective statement timeout before it reaches production scale.
ai_value: Helps agents recognize that a read-only aggregate can create a production outage when distinct counts are computed over a blown-up join graph.

applies_to.ecosystem: relational applications with products, options, variants, dimensions, permissions, tags, or other many-to-many structures
contexts: a list or dashboard endpoint displays both real entity counts and maximum combination counts
multiple one-to-many tables are joined before count(distinct ...) or grouped aggregates
the data model intentionally has sparse real rows plus a larger logical grid
a UI request or polling endpoint runs the aggregate repeatedly

trigger_signals.description: The SQL joins axes, values, cells, products, or other many-to-many dimensions and then calls count(distinct ...) over the joined result.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Assume the query may be multiplying rows before counting; inspect the plan at realistic scale before shipping.

trigger_signals.description: Database CPU spikes from a read-only list/count endpoint, while terminating the aggregate queries immediately relieves load.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat the count query itself as the incident source, not merely as harmless observability.

trigger_signals.description: The product model distinguishes sparse real entities from a larger logical cartesian grid.
trigger_signals.pattern: sparse|logical grid|actual rows|max combinations|variant dimensions|option axes
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Compute sparse entity counts and logical-grid counts in separate subqueries or pre-aggregates instead of one broad joined aggregate.

negative_signals.description: The joined relations are provably tiny, bounded, and protected by tests or database constraints that prevent multiplication.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The cartesian risk depends on scale and join cardinality, not on the syntax alone.

negative_signals.description: The count runs only in an operator-gated offline diagnostic with a timeout and no user-facing refresh loop.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: One-off diagnostics have a different risk profile from hot production endpoints.

common_wrong_assumptions: A read-only count cannot be the cause of an outage.
count(distinct ...) makes a broad join safe because duplicates are removed at the end.
The logical combination count and real sparse row count should be computed in the same joined query.
Adding more indexes will fix a query whose main cost is row multiplication.

first_checks.check: Run EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the count query at realistic scale and inspect estimated versus actual rows at each join.
first_checks.why: The dangerous clue is often a large intermediate row count before the final distinct aggregate.

first_checks.check: Rewrite counts as independent CTEs or pre-aggregates: count real sparse rows in one branch and logical combinations from dimension cardinalities in another branch.
first_checks.why: Pre-aggregation prevents the database from building the full cartesian join just to discard duplicates later.

first_checks.check: Verify the effective timeout layer by forcing a deliberately slow version in a safe environment and confirming the application receives a bounded failure.
first_checks.why: Timeouts are useful only if applied on the connection/session/query layer actually used by the endpoint.

decision_rules.condition: A hot endpoint joins multiple many-to-many dimensions before count(distinct ...), and the UI only needs separate sparse and logical counts.
decision_rules.then: Use CTEs or independent subqueries, compare before/after plans and runtime, and keep a statement timeout guard on the production path.

do_not: Do not rely on count(distinct ...) to rescue a query after a broad cartesian join has already happened.
Do not ship a production list endpoint aggregate without checking cardinality at realistic data scale.
Do not remove timeout guards after the query is optimized; keep bounded failure for regression safety.
Do not publish private product names, URLs, tenant identifiers, repository paths, database names, or incident timestamps beyond de-identified evidence.
Do not merge this with hot-count-polling-can-become-the-incident or page-before-expensive-aggregation; they are related count-load traps with different mechanisms.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When adding counts over variant/dimension structures, design the count query from cardinalities and sparse facts separately, then prove the plan does not materialize the full combination space.

risk.notes: Candidate is based on one private production-backed incident and should be independently reviewed and de-identified before publication.

sources.supports: A production endpoint used distinct counts over a joined option-composition graph, causing sustained database CPU saturation. Terminating the active read queries relieved load; splitting the aggregate into CTEs reduced runtime from minutes to seconds, and a timeout guard was added.

title: Page before expensive aggregation on large list screens
summary: On large list screens, filter and page candidate IDs before running expensive detail joins, window counts, or aggregates; make has-more and approximate totals explicit product contracts.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid turning read-only list views into production load by aggregating the whole result set before bounding the page.

contexts: a list screen joins detail tables or computes aggregate counts for every matching row
the UI only needs the current page plus a has-more signal
agents are tempted to preserve exact total counts while adding filters or hotfixes

trigger_signals.description: The query computes window counts, detail joins, or aggregates before LIMIT/OFFSET or cursor paging.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Move to a two-phase query: cheap candidate IDs first, expensive work only for the selected page.

trigger_signals.description: The UI demands an exact total even though the operation is primarily page navigation.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat exactness as a product contract; use limit+1 has-more or labelled approximations if acceptable.

trigger_signals.description: EXPLAIN shows large intermediate rows for a screen that displays only a small page.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The page boundary is in the wrong phase.

negative_signals.description: The product explicitly requires a globally exact total before showing any page.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then keep the exact count but budget it, cache it, or run it off the hot request path.

negative_signals.description: The filtered candidate set is already small and bounded before aggregates run.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The additional two-phase machinery may not be necessary.

common_wrong_assumptions: A read-only list query is safe because it does not mutate data.
LIMIT at the end protects every earlier aggregate.
Exact total counts are harmless UI polish.

first_checks.check: Run EXPLAIN or ORM logging and identify whether candidate IDs are bounded before detail joins and aggregates.
first_checks.why: The expensive phase should operate on the page, not the whole match set.

first_checks.check: Prototype a limit+1 candidate-ID query and compare latency at realistic filter cardinality.
first_checks.why: Limit+1 proves has-more without a global count.

first_checks.check: Review UI copy for exact-total claims.
first_checks.why: Changing an exact number to approximate or has-more is a user-visible contract change, not a hidden performance patch.

decision_rules.condition: Expensive joins or aggregates run before the page boundary.
decision_rules.then: Filter and sort cheap candidate IDs, fetch limit+1, then join or aggregate only those IDs.

decision_rules.condition: The exact global count is not required for the user decision.
decision_rules.then: Expose has_more or an explicitly labelled approximation instead of a hot exact count.

decision_rules.condition: Exact totals are required and expensive.
decision_rules.then: Cache, precompute, or run the exact count in a separately budgeted path.

do_not: Do not run detail joins, window counts, or aggregates across an unbounded list because the final page is small.
Do not silently replace exact totals with approximate labels without changing the UI contract.
Do not treat this as the same trap as hot polling or cartesian join blow-up; cross-check those records separately.

Do not collapse this with hot-count-polling-can-become-the-incident or cartesian-distinct-counts-can-dos-a-production-db; this record is specifically about paging candidate IDs before detail aggregation.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Inspect the query phase order and move the page boundary before expensive aggregation when the screen only needs one page.

risk.notes: This record is de-identified agent guidance. It does not authorize bypassing maintainer, security, publication, production, billing, data, permission, or destructive-action gates.

title: Mail provider DNS screens are not authoritative DNS
summary: When diagnosing SPF, DKIM, DMARC, or MX failures, an agent can mistake a mail host or SaaS control panel that displays generated DNS records for the place where public DNS is actually served. The control panel may be correct locally while the authoritative registrar/DNS provider has no matching public record.
ai_value: Prevents agents from chasing application credentials, code, or propagation guesses before proving which DNS provider is authoritative for the queried name.

contexts: Email deliverability, SMTP envelope, POP/IMAP, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, or MX diagnostics
SaaS or hosting panels that generate DNS records while a different registrar or DNS provider serves the zone
Agents deciding whether a domain authentication failure is a code bug, provider rejection, or DNS publication issue

trigger_signals.description: A provider UI says SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MX, or a selector exists, but external checks or message headers still show missing or failing authentication.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Split generated settings from publicly served DNS and query the authoritative nameservers directly.

trigger_signals.description: The team is about to rotate credentials, change mail code, or add workarounds because a DNS-backed mail check fails.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: First prove authoritative DNS state; otherwise the proposed fix may be irrelevant and riskier than the root cause.

negative_signals.description: The provider shown in the UI is also confirmed as an authoritative nameserver for the exact zone or delegated subdomain.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then the provider UI may be a valid source of public DNS truth, though external query verification is still useful.

negative_signals.description: External authoritative DNS queries show the required record and message headers still fail for a different reason.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then the remaining problem is more likely alignment, selector mismatch, provider signing, SMTP envelope, or application configuration.

common_wrong_assumptions: A mail host control panel that displays a DKIM key has published that key to the public Internet.
A DNS checker in one vendor console is enough evidence for every subdomain and selector.
If authentication fails after a record was entered somewhere, the next step is credential or application debugging.
DNS propagation is the default explanation before checking delegation and authoritative nameservers.

first_checks.check: Find the authoritative nameservers for the exact domain or subdomain being tested.
first_checks.why: Only the authoritative DNS provider determines what public resolvers can see.
first_checks.command: dig NS example.com +short; dig TXT selector._domainkey.example.com @<authoritative-ns>

first_checks.check: Compare the record host/name expected by the provider with the host/name actually queried in headers or diagnostics.
first_checks.why: DKIM selector and subdomain mistakes can look like unpublished DNS even when some related record exists.

first_checks.check: After publication, verify through both authoritative query and a fresh message header or provider test.
first_checks.why: The record existing in DNS and the mail system using/aliging it are separate facts.

decision_rules.condition: The generated DNS record is visible in a vendor UI but absent from authoritative DNS.
decision_rules.then: Publish the record at the authoritative provider or correct delegation; do not rotate credentials or patch application mail logic for this symptom.

decision_rules.condition: The operation would mutate production DNS, credentials, mail routing, or delivery policy.
decision_rules.then: Stop at the relevant operational gate and present the authoritative-query evidence and exact record names.

do_not: Do not treat a generated DNS record shown in a mail/SaaS panel as proof of public DNS publication.
Do not change application credentials or mail code before checking authoritative nameservers when the symptom is DNS-backed authentication failure.
Do not paste private domains, selectors, account names, or provider console screenshots into public lessons.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: For mail authentication failures, first identify authoritative DNS and query the exact MX/TXT/selector record there; then decide whether the fix is DNS publication, provider signing/alignment, or application behavior.

risk.notes: DNS, credentials, and mail-routing changes can affect live delivery. This candidate only guides diagnosis and does not authorize production DNS or secret mutation.

sources.supports: A private mail-recovery session found that a hosting/mail UI displayed generated authentication records while the authoritative DNS provider was elsewhere; public DKIM/SPF state only changed after records were added at the authoritative provider.

title: Mailbox folder moves are not retention or provider deletion
summary: Mailbox folder moves, retention reservations, and provider-side deletion are separate state transitions. Prove each with count evidence before treating a move request as destructive retention or delete work.
ai_value: Prevents agents from turning a reversible visibility/routing change into data loss or provider-side mutation while still honoring explicit folder-routing intent.

contexts: Applications that ingest, classify, or bulk-move email into mailbox folders
Spam, quarantine, archive, trash, or server-delete staging features
Live-data cleanup scripts that translate tags, labels, rules, or assessments into folder state

trigger_signals.description: A human says to move mail to a spam, archive, trash, or quarantine folder, and the code or cleanup plan also touches retention, scheduled deletion, provider delete state, or server-side delete reservations.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Split the requested folder move from every deletion or retention effect before applying changes.

trigger_signals.description: A live cleanup converts a tag, label, or classifier result into folder membership for many existing messages.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Count source labels and destination-folder inventory, then verify that stale delete/staging state is either intentionally preserved or intentionally cleared.

negative_signals.description: The change only updates an internal folder pointer or visible label and tests show it does not enqueue deletion, update provider delete state, or shorten retention.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A reversible mailbox organization change is usually lower risk than a deletion or provider mutation, though live data still needs normal safeguards.

negative_signals.description: A separate reviewed policy explicitly authorizes the retention period, delete scope, provider-side mutation, recovery path, and verification evidence.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The trap is accidental bundling; explicit deletion policy can proceed through the appropriate gate.

common_wrong_assumptions: A request to move mail between folders automatically includes retention changes or provider-side deletion.
Putting a message in a spam folder means it should also be scheduled for deletion.
A cleanup from spam labels to spam folders should preserve or create server-delete reservations by default.
Trash, spam, quarantine, and provider-side delete are equivalent because the UI hides the message from the inbox.
If a folder move is reversible in the app, provider-side deletion is also safe to include.
Source tag counts are enough for a live cleanup review without destination-folder inventory and delete-state counts.

first_checks.check: List every data field, queue, job, or provider call that can delete, purge, expire, or hide the message outside the requested folder move.
first_checks.why: Folder state and deletion state often live in different tables or workers; a cleanup can accidentally carry both.

first_checks.check: Before live cleanup, count source labels/tags, destination folder inventory, existing delete reservations, and rows with both old and new states.
first_checks.why: These counts prove whether the plan is a move, a duplicate state, or a deletion-state mutation.

first_checks.check: After the transaction, verify moved count, remaining source links, destination count delta, and delete reservation count delta.
first_checks.why: Post-checks catch partial moves and accidental retention/deletion side effects.

decision_rules.condition: The user asked for a folder move but did not explicitly authorize deletion, retention expiry, or provider-side mutation.
decision_rules.then: Move the messages within the mailbox model, preserve recoverability, and do not enqueue provider/server deletion unless a separate gate authorizes it.

decision_rules.condition: The cleanup plan would preserve, create, or execute delete reservations for messages being moved to a non-delete folder.
decision_rules.then: Stop and present counts for source labels, target folder, and delete reservations; require explicit deletion/retention policy before proceeding with delete effects.

decision_rules.condition: A reviewed policy explicitly asks for retention or provider deletion after foldering.
decision_rules.then: Run the normal hard-gate path with retention duration, scope, dry-run counts, rollback/recovery limits, and post-apply verification.

do_not: Do not infer provider-side deletion from a request to move messages into a spam, archive, trash, or quarantine folder.
Do not combine label-to-folder cleanup with retention or server-delete changes unless the delete semantics are explicitly authorized.
Do not review a live mail cleanup using only source label counts; include target folder inventory and delete-state counts.
Do not publish private mailbox domains, account names, message subjects, or customer data in public lessons.
Do not merge this with uncertain-spam visibility policy; cross-check uncertain-spam-signals-should-not-hide-customer-mail when signal confidence is the issue.
Do not over-read a human request scope; compare ambiguous-human-input-overauthorization when authorization wording is ambiguous.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When mail foldering and deletion are both present, split the plan into visibility/folder state, retention policy, and provider mutation; verify counts for each before writing live data.

risk.notes: Provider deletion, retention changes, and live mailbox cleanup can cause data loss. This candidate only guides separation of effects and does not authorize destructive mail changes.

sources.supports: A private mail cleanup session distinguished an operator-requested spam-folder move from automatic deletion and provider/server delete reservations; the safe path moved messages to the folder, removed obsolete label/link state, and did not add deletion behavior.

title: Uncertain spam signals should not hide customer mail
summary: When agents add spam protection to a customer-facing mailbox, they may treat authentication failures, sender reputation hints, or broad content keywords as enough evidence to auto-quarantine messages. For unknown external senders, those signals are uncertain; hiding mail can lose legitimate customer contact. Keep uncertain detections visible as labels, shadow scores, or audit events until a stricter business policy and verification gate exists.
ai_value: Prevents agents from converting detection logic into message-hiding behavior before proving that the signal is definitive enough for the mailbox's customer-communication risk.

contexts: Applications that ingest or display customer-facing email in a mailbox, CRM, helpdesk, marketplace, or support workflow
Spam or abuse classifiers based on SPF, DKIM, DMARC, sender domain, content keywords, user reports, or external reputation signals
Rule engines or settings tables that can label, move, hide, quarantine, retain, or delete mail

trigger_signals.description: A new spam feature can move, hide, quarantine, or delete messages from unknown external senders based on authentication failure or missing authentication alone.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat this as a customer-mail visibility gate, not just a classifier implementation detail.

trigger_signals.description: A database setting or admin mode says quarantine, but code and API gates do not independently hold or reject quarantine for uncertain signals.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Storage shape must not be enough to activate message-hiding behavior.

trigger_signals.description: Trusted-domain or own-domain configuration is editable or data-driven and could silently widen self-spoof quarantine beyond the explicitly launched domain set.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Prove a launch allowlist or equivalent policy boundary prevents accidental scope expansion.

negative_signals.description: The action only adds a visible label, score, audit entry, or shadow-mode assessment and does not move, hide, suppress, retain, or delete the message.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Detection-only work can usually proceed with ordinary validation because customer visibility is preserved.

negative_signals.description: The message is a definitive own-domain self-spoof under a reviewed allowlist and failed/missing authentication condition, or the exact sender was manually blocked by an authorized user action.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Some narrow cases can be strong enough for quarantine when tests prove the boundary and no broader customer-mail rule is activated.

negative_signals.description: A reviewed policy explicitly authorizes the exact sender class, signal class, mailbox, retention behavior, and user-visible recovery path for quarantine or deletion.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The trap targets accidental or premature quarantine, not execution of a precise approved policy.

common_wrong_assumptions: Authentication failure from an external domain always means the message is spam.
If a setting row says quarantine, the feature is safe to activate without code-level launch holds.
Broad content words in subject or body are enough to move customer mail out of the inbox.
Adding a spam folder is reversible enough that no owner or business policy gate is needed.
A trusted-domain table can double as the production allowlist for self-spoof quarantine without a separate launch boundary.

first_checks.check: Enumerate every code path that can move, hide, quarantine, suppress, retain, or delete mail, including rule execution, API settings, scheduled jobs, and manual actions.
first_checks.why: Spam classifiers often have multiple effect paths; a safe label-only path can be bypassed by a settings or worker path.

first_checks.check: Add negative fixtures for unknown external senders with failed, missing, or misaligned authentication and spammy-looking content.
first_checks.why: These fixtures should remain visible in the inbox or normal mail list unless a reviewed policy says otherwise.

first_checks.check: Add positive fixtures only for definitive cases, such as own-domain self-spoof constrained by an explicit allowlist, and exact-sender manual blocks.
first_checks.why: Positive tests should prove the narrow live behavior without broadening uncertain external-domain quarantine.

first_checks.check: Test that database settings, admin API updates, and rule-engine execution all reject or hold general quarantine while policy is pending.
first_checks.why: A database mode can become an accidental feature flag if enforcement exists in only one layer.

decision_rules.condition: A signal is uncertain and the sender may be a legitimate external customer.
decision_rules.then: Keep the message visible and record the assessment as a label, score, audit event, or shadow decision instead of moving or hiding it.

decision_rules.condition: A setting, API, or rule action would enable general quarantine, retention, or deletion before policy approval.
decision_rules.then: Stop before activation and ask for the exact sender class, mailbox scope, retention/delete semantics, recovery path, and monitoring requirement.

decision_rules.condition: The case is definitive own-domain self-spoof and an explicit launch allowlist plus failed/missing authentication are both proven by tests.
decision_rules.then: Allow the narrow quarantine path while keeping external-domain and non-allowlisted-domain cases label-only or shadow.

decision_rules.condition: The behavior is a user-initiated exact-sender block or manual spam action.
decision_rules.then: Confirm the action is exact-sender scoped, auditable, and reversible through the product's normal user/admin controls before relying on it as a live path.

do_not: Do not auto-quarantine unknown external-domain mail solely because SPF, DKIM, or DMARC failed or is missing.
Do not turn a database quarantine mode into live behavior unless API and rule execution layers enforce the same policy boundary.
Do not let trusted-domain rows silently expand own-domain self-spoof quarantine beyond an explicit launch allowlist.
Do not infer deletion, retention, or permanent suppression semantics from a quarantine feature request.
Do not hide customer-visible mail with broad keyword classifiers unless the exact policy and recovery path have been reviewed.
Do not use this signal-confidence record to decide retention or provider deletion semantics; cross-check mailbox-folder-move-is-not-retention-or-provider-delete for count-evidence effect separation.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Before enabling any mail-hiding action, classify each signal as definitive or uncertain, prove uncertain cases remain visible, and gate quarantine/deletion semantics through the exact reviewed policy.

risk.notes: This trap protects customer communications and potential data-loss/visibility boundaries. It does not authorize changing production mail routing, retention, deletion, security, or permission behavior without the applicable reviewed or human gate.

sources.supports: A de-identified production mail-spam implementation found that database quarantine mode and trusted-domain data could have widened live quarantine unless code/API launch holds and allowlist filtering were enforced. The safe result kept uncertain external-domain spam label-only/shadow while allowing only narrow definitive self-spoof and manual exact-sender block paths.

title: Dropdown form submits can vanish when the menu unmounts
summary: A native form placed inside a dropdown, popover, command menu, or context menu can lose its submit path if the menu closes and unmounts before the browser or framework dispatches the submit/mutation. The UI may look clicked while no API request is sent.
ai_value: Helps agents diagnose missing mutations in menu-driven UI actions without over-focusing on backend routes, auth, or validation when the frontend never sent the request.

contexts: React, Vue, Svelte, or similar component UIs with dropdown, popover, context-menu, command-menu, or modal actions
Menu items implemented as forms, submit buttons, server actions, or framework action helpers
User reports that clicking a menu action closes the menu but produces no backend effect

trigger_signals.description: A button or menu item closes a dropdown immediately and no network request appears for the intended action.
trigger_signals.pattern: dropdown|popover|menu|context menu|no request|no API call|submit|form action
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Inspect whether the form or submit button unmounts before submit/mutation dispatch.

trigger_signals.description: Backend route, validation, and auth tests pass, but the real UI action has no server log or request trace.
trigger_signals.pattern: route passes|server action works|no server log|clicked but nothing happened
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Suspect frontend event lifetime or component unmount rather than backend behavior.

negative_signals.description: The network request is sent and receives a 4xx/5xx or validation response.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Then the problem is downstream of event dispatch, such as auth, payload shape, validation, or backend logic.

negative_signals.description: The menu component keeps the form mounted until the submit promise is started or awaited, and tests prove the request fires before close.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Unmount loss is unlikely when lifecycle ordering is explicitly controlled and verified.

common_wrong_assumptions: If a submit button was clicked, the browser definitely sent the form submit.
A menu closing after click means the action succeeded or at least reached the backend.
Missing mutation effects are most likely a route, auth, or database bug.
Native forms are always safer than explicit fetch calls inside transient menu components.

first_checks.check: Use the browser network tab or test mock to prove whether the action request is sent before debugging the backend.
first_checks.why: A vanished submit leaves no request; backend inspection cannot explain an event that never left the client.

first_checks.check: Inspect whether the menu closes, route changes, or state update unmounts the form synchronously in the same click path.
first_checks.why: Transient component lifecycle can interrupt native form/server-action submission.

first_checks.check: Add a regression test that clicks the actual menu item and asserts the mutation function or network request is called.
first_checks.why: Route-only tests miss the frontend event lifetime bug.

decision_rules.condition: The menu action unmounts the form before a submit or mutation is observed.
decision_rules.then: Use an explicit click handler/fetch/server-action call that starts before closing the menu, or defer menu close until submit has been dispatched/awaited.

decision_rules.condition: A regression test only exercises the backend route or action helper directly.
decision_rules.then: Add a component or browser test that opens the dropdown, clicks the menu action, and observes the request/mutation call.

do_not: Do not assume a clicked native form inside a transient dropdown sent a request unless the network/log evidence shows it.
Do not debug backend persistence first when the UI action has no request trace.
Do not expose private UI labels, account names, URLs, or customer data in public candidate examples.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When a dropdown/menu action appears to do nothing, prove request dispatch in the actual UI path; if absent, make mutation dispatch explicit or keep the form mounted through submit.

risk.notes: This is a frontend event-lifecycle trap. Production mutations, auth, data deletion, or customer-visible behavior changes still need their ordinary gates.

sources.supports: A private frontend session found that menu-contained native forms closed/unmounted before submit reached the API; replacing the path with explicit request dispatch fixed the missing mutation.

title: Next.js instrumentation hooks need exclusion guards and thin dependencies
summary: Framework instrumentation hooks run in constrained startup contexts. Guard unsupported runtimes by exclusion, keep the hook thin, and prove it fires once in a production-equivalent start.
ai_value: Helps agents avoid bundling server-only runner graphs into framework startup hooks or skipping runtimes because an expected runtime variable is undefined.

contexts: a Next.js app adds or changes instrumentation startup hooks
the hook may execute in node and edge-like runtime contexts
the hook imports job runners, database clients, or other server-only graphs

trigger_signals.description: The guard only runs when a runtime value equals the expected supported runtime.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Guard by excluding known unsupported runtimes; an undefined value may still be the desired server runtime.

trigger_signals.description: The hook imports a large runner graph or server-only modules directly.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Move the heavy dependency behind a thin dynamic boundary or runtime-specific loader.

trigger_signals.description: Build or startup errors mention unsupported schemes or runtime-only modules from the hook path.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Treat the hook as a constrained startup surface, not a normal application module.

negative_signals.description: The hook is pure telemetry with no runtime-specific imports and has an explicit supported-runtime contract.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The thin-hook trap may not apply, but still verify single-fire startup behavior.

negative_signals.description: Processed-count stillness occurs during a long transaction in an import job.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: That is an import progress signal, not an instrumentation stall; see progress-state-must-match-cursor-semantics.

common_wrong_assumptions: A startup hook can import anything a normal server route can import.
Undefined runtime means the hook is not running in the supported runtime.
A successful build proves the hook fires exactly once at startup.

first_checks.check: Build after adding or changing the instrumentation hook.
first_checks.why: Import-graph and runtime-boundary failures often surface only at build time.

first_checks.check: Start the app in the closest production-equivalent mode and verify the hook fires once.
first_checks.why: Development hot reload can hide missing or repeated startup behavior.

first_checks.check: Review imports from the hook entrypoint and move heavy/server-only graphs behind thin adapters.
first_checks.why: Thin hooks reduce runtime compatibility failures.

decision_rules.condition: The hook must skip unsupported runtimes.
decision_rules.then: Skip known unsupported runtime values and allow unspecified supported server startup when the framework uses that convention.

decision_rules.condition: The hook imports heavy or server-only implementation graphs.
decision_rules.then: Keep the hook as a small dispatcher and load runtime-specific work only inside the supported runtime.

decision_rules.condition: The hook cannot be proven to fire once in production-equivalent mode.
decision_rules.then: Add a safe diagnostic marker or test until single-fire startup behavior is observed.

do_not: Do not bundle background job runners or server-only module graphs directly into instrumentation startup hooks.
Do not assume positive runtime detection is reliable when the framework may leave it undefined.
Do not keep unrelated lease or import-resume lessons in this record; link those records instead.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Inspect the instrumentation hook as a constrained startup surface: exclusion guard, thin imports, production-equivalent single-fire proof.

risk.notes: This record is de-identified agent guidance. It does not authorize bypassing maintainer, security, publication, production, billing, data, permission, or destructive-action gates.

sources.supports: Item 21 was conditionally selected after narrowing to guard-by-exclusion and thin instrumentation hooks. The reshape provides three trigger signals, so it was published.

title: Detached HEAD work must be anchored to a branch before normal push
summary: Agents may make commits while Git is in detached HEAD state, then fail or loop when `git push` cannot infer a branch. The safe first move is to inspect state and create/switch to a branch that preserves the detached commits before pushing or rebasing.
ai_value: Prevents agents from losing work or applying destructive Git commands when a commit exists outside a named branch. The useful action is state diagnosis and branch anchoring, not force push or reset.

contexts: repository is in detached HEAD state
agent has local commits or changes it wants to preserve
normal git push fails because no current branch exists

trigger_signals.description: Short branch status shows HEAD with no branch.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Do not assume the agent is on main/master/current feature branch; detached commits may not be reachable by a branch.

trigger_signals.description: Plain git push fails because there is no current branch.
trigger_signals.pattern: fatal: You are not currently on a branch\.|To push the history leading to the current \(detached HEAD\) state now
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The next safe action is to preserve the current HEAD on a named branch, not to retry push blindly.

trigger_signals.description: git branch --show-current prints an empty line.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Empty current branch output is consistent with detached HEAD; confirm with status before branch operations.

negative_signals.description: git branch --show-current prints a non-empty branch name.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: If Git is already on a branch, this detached-HEAD recovery trap may not apply; handle upstream/push configuration separately.

negative_signals.description: The repository has no commits yet or is on an unborn branch.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Unborn branch setup is a different Git initialization case, not detached HEAD recovery.

common_wrong_assumptions: The current commit must already belong to main or the last visible branch.
Retrying git push with different remote names will fix detached HEAD.
A force push, hard reset, or checkout is a safe first response.
Detached HEAD means the work is lost.

first_checks.check: Inspect the branch/detached state without modifying files.
first_checks.why: Agents must know whether HEAD is attached before choosing a push or branch operation.

first_checks.check: Check the current branch name.
first_checks.why: An empty output from git branch --show-current is a simple detached HEAD signal.

first_checks.check: Show recent commits and refs that may need preservation.
first_checks.why: Before creating/switching branches, identify whether current HEAD contains work not on an existing branch.

decision_rules.condition: Git status shows detached HEAD and the current HEAD contains work that should be kept.
decision_rules.then: Create a new branch at the current commit with `git switch -c <safe-branch-name>` before pushing or opening a PR. Choose a descriptive branch name; do not discard changes.

decision_rules.condition: Git is detached only for temporary inspection and there is no work to keep.
decision_rules.then: Switch back to the intended branch with `git switch <branch>` or `git switch -`; avoid carrying unreviewed detached-state assumptions into later commands.

decision_rules.condition: There are uncommitted changes and switching/branching may conflict.
decision_rules.then: Stop before using stash, reset, checkout, or discard-style options unless the owner explicitly approves the data-loss risk.

do_not: Do not run `git reset --hard`, `git switch --discard-changes`, or equivalent destructive commands as the first response.
Do not force push from detached HEAD to an existing protected branch.
Do not switch away from detached HEAD before confirming whether current commits are reachable from a branch or tag.
Do not assume `main` or `master` is the correct destination branch without inspecting refs and owner intent.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Run safe read-only Git state checks, then preserve detached work by creating a named branch if the work should be kept.

risk.notes: Branch creation is usually safe, but reset/discard/force-push operations can lose work or rewrite shared history and require a gate.

sources.excerpt: Git status porcelain v2 branch headers include branch.head, which can be a branch or detached.
sources.supports: Official git-status documentation describes branch headers that identify current branch or detached state.

sources.excerpt: git switch changes branches and updates working tree/index to match the branch.
sources.supports: Official git-switch documentation describes switching to branches.

sources.excerpt: git switch -c creates a new branch at a start point and switches to it.
sources.supports: Official git-switch documentation describes creating and switching to a new branch.

sources.excerpt: git switch --detach switches to a commit for inspection or discardable experiments; if work is worth keeping, create a new name for it.
sources.supports: Official git-switch documentation describes detached HEAD and creating a branch to keep work.

sources.excerpt: git switch - can switch back to the previous branch.
sources.supports: Official git-switch documentation describes switching back to the previous branch.

sources.excerpt: git switch refuses operations that would lose local changes unless told otherwise with discard/merge options.
sources.supports: Official git-switch documentation describes local-change preservation and discard options.

sources.excerpt: Local reproduction showed `## HEAD (no branch)` and `fatal: You are not currently on a branch` after committing in detached HEAD state and running plain git push.
sources.supports: Local verification confirms the trigger signals and push failure in a detached HEAD state with a configured remote.

verification_runs.command: Create a temporary git repo and bare remote, commit on main, switch --detach to an earlier commit, commit detached work, then run git status --short --branch, git branch --show-current, and git push.
verification_runs.observed_result: git status --short --branch printed `## HEAD (no branch)`; git branch --show-current printed an empty line; plain git push printed `fatal: You are not currently on a branch` with advice to push HEAD to a named remote branch.
verification_runs.conclusion: Detached HEAD work is not on a normal current branch, so an agent should preserve it with a named branch before ordinary push/PR workflow.

title: Bun module mocks can leak across same-process test files
summary: When multiple Bun test files run in one process, a module-level mock introduced for one test file can affect another file that imports the same module, creating false failures outside the intended test scope.
ai_value: Before adding broad module mocks to prove a scheduler or orchestrator path, agents should check whether sibling tests import the mocked module in the same Bun process and choose an isolated test/process or dependency injection instead.

contexts: Bun test suites that run multiple files in one process
Tests using module-level mocks for a module imported by other test files

trigger_signals.description: A new test file uses a module-level mock for a local service module, and unrelated tests that import that service begin failing in the same test command.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Suspect cross-file mock pollution before changing production code or weakening assertions.

trigger_signals.description: The failure disappears when the mocked test is run separately or when the module mock is removed.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The mocked module may be shared through Bun's module cache across files in that process.

negative_signals.description: The mocked module is not imported by any other test file in the same process.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The cross-file pollution trap is less likely when there is no shared import boundary.

negative_signals.description: The failure reproduces when the affected test file is run alone without the mocking test file.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A standalone reproduction points to a real issue in that test or source path, not only mock leakage.

common_wrong_assumptions: A module mock declared in one Bun test file is automatically isolated from every other test file in the same command.
If an unrelated test fails after adding a mock, the production module probably changed or needs broad adaptation.
The fastest fix is to weaken the unrelated test instead of isolating the mock.

first_checks.check: Run the newly mocked test file by itself and then with the failing sibling test file.
first_checks.why: A pairwise rerun distinguishes a local test failure from same-process mock pollution.

first_checks.check: Search for imports of the mocked module across the selected test files.
first_checks.why: Shared imports identify the module cache boundary that can carry the mock.

decision_rules.condition: The failure appears only when the mocking test and another importer run together.
decision_rules.then: Move the proof into an isolated test process/file selection, avoid mocking the shared module, or refactor the code under test to accept injectable dependencies.

decision_rules.condition: The sibling test fails even when run alone without the mocking test.
decision_rules.then: Treat it as a real source or test defect and debug normally rather than blaming mock leakage.

do_not: Do not leave a broad module mock in a shared same-process test bundle without proving isolation.
Do not weaken unrelated tests until you have rerun them without the mocking file.
Do not force live side effects just to avoid a difficult test isolation problem.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When unrelated Bun tests fail after adding a module mock, rerun the mocking test alone and paired with the failing file, then isolate the mock or use dependency injection.

risk.notes: The candidate is based on one private dogfooding case and should be reviewed with a public fixture or second independent case before promotion. Confidence caveat: this is a reviewed, self-verifying runtime-behavior heuristic from a private incident, not a universal claim about all Bun versions; rerun the pairwise isolation checks in the target repository.

sources.supports: A scheduler test that mocked a local service module caused false failures in another service test when both files ran in the same Bun test command; removing or isolating the mock resolved the issue.

title: Modern Node CJS require(esm) may return a namespace object, not ERR_REQUIRE_ESM
summary: Agents often claim that requiring an ESM-only package from CommonJS always throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM. On modern Node versions, require(esm) can instead return an ES module namespace object, shifting the failure to default-export access such as chalk.blue is not a function.
ai_value: Before changing module systems or pinning old packages, an agent should inspect Node version, resolved package version, and the actual require() return shape.

contexts: CommonJS entrypoint using require()
package.json without type: module

trigger_signals.description: CommonJS code calls require('chalk') and then chalk.blue(...) while package metadata resolves chalk@5+.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Do not assume the only possible failure is ERR_REQUIRE_ESM; inspect the returned module shape and Node version.

trigger_signals.description: Runtime error says TypeError: chalk.blue is not a function.
trigger_signals.pattern: TypeError: chalk\.blue is not a function
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: This may be a namespace/default export mismatch rather than a plain missing dependency.

negative_signals.description: The project already imports chalk using ESM import syntax.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The CJS require namespace trap may not apply if the callsite is already ESM.

negative_signals.description: The installed chalk version is v4 or lower.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: chalk v4 is CommonJS-compatible, so this specific chalk@5 require(esm) trap is likely not the cause.

common_wrong_assumptions: All ESM-only packages always fail from CJS with ERR_REQUIRE_ESM.
The correct fix is always to pin chalk to v4.
If require('chalk') does not throw, then chalk.blue must be available as a top-level property.

first_checks.check: Check the active Node version.
first_checks.why: Node's CJS/ESM interop behavior changes by version.

first_checks.check: Check the installed package version and resolved package metadata.
first_checks.why: The same package name can have CJS and ESM-major versions.

first_checks.check: Inspect what require() actually returns before rewriting broad module settings.
first_checks.why: Modern Node may return a namespace object with a default export.

decision_rules.condition: require('chalk') returns an object with a callable default export and code uses chalk.blue(...).
decision_rules.then: Use the default export shape, migrate this callsite to import syntax, or convert the project/module boundary intentionally; do not diagnose this as a plain ERR_REQUIRE_ESM case.

decision_rules.condition: The runtime actually throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM.
decision_rules.then: Use dynamic import(), migrate the relevant module to ESM, or pin a CJS-compatible version only as an explicit compatibility tradeoff.

do_not: Do not state that CJS require() of ESM always throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM without checking Node version.
Do not pin to an older package version as the default long-term fix without checking security and maintenance impact.
Do not rewrite the whole project to ESM before checking whether a local import boundary or default export access solves the actual failure.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: Diagnose the active Node version, installed package version, and require() return shape before changing dependencies or module settings.

risk.notes: Changing module system broadly or pinning packages can create project-wide churn; keep the first action diagnostic.

sources.excerpt: Node.js official documentation section on interoperability with CommonJS.
sources.supports: Node documents interoperability boundaries between ECMAScript modules and CommonJS.

sources.excerpt: Node.js official documentation section on loading ECMAScript modules using require().
sources.supports: Node documents loading ECMAScript modules using require() under supported conditions.

sources.supports: Local verification observed chalk@5.6.2 under Node v22.22.2 returning a namespace object and failing at chalk.blue access.

title: Pydantic v2 moved BaseSettings to pydantic-settings
summary: Agents often use Pydantic v1 examples and write `from pydantic import BaseSettings`. With Pydantic v2 this raises PydanticImportError because BaseSettings moved to the separate `pydantic-settings` package.
ai_value: Before downgrading Pydantic or rewriting settings code broadly, an agent should check the installed Pydantic major version, whether pydantic-settings is installed, and update the import path for v2 projects.

contexts: Python project imports BaseSettings from pydantic
Pydantic v2 is installed or resolved by dependency solver
Application uses environment/settings management

trigger_signals.description: Python code imports BaseSettings directly from pydantic while pydantic resolves to v2.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Do not assume Pydantic v1 import paths still apply; check whether pydantic-settings should be used.

trigger_signals.description: Runtime error says BaseSettings has been moved to the pydantic-settings package.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The immediate diagnosis is Pydantic v2 settings-package split, not a generic missing module or Python path problem.

negative_signals.description: The project intentionally pins Pydantic v1 and import succeeds in the active environment.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: Pydantic v1 still exposes BaseSettings from pydantic; this v2 migration trap may not apply. Avoid unnecessary dependency churn.

negative_signals.description: The code already imports BaseSettings from pydantic_settings.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: If the v2 import path is already used, the failure is likely elsewhere, such as package installation, environment mismatch, or settings field validation.

common_wrong_assumptions: Pydantic v1 examples remain valid for Pydantic v2 projects.
The fix is always to downgrade pydantic to v1.
PydanticImportError means pydantic itself is missing or the Python path is broken.
Installing pydantic alone is enough for BaseSettings in v2.

first_checks.check: Check the active Python and Pydantic versions in the same environment that fails.
first_checks.why: Dependency solvers and IDEs may use a different environment than the failing runtime.
first_checks.command:
python - <<'PY'
import sys, pydantic
print(sys.executable)
print(sys.version.split()[0])
print(pydantic.__version__)
PY

first_checks.check: Search for the old BaseSettings import path.
first_checks.why: The old import path is the direct trigger for this Pydantic v2 failure.

first_checks.check: Check whether pydantic-settings is installed in the failing environment.
first_checks.why: Pydantic v2 settings management lives in a separate package.

decision_rules.condition: Pydantic v2 is installed and code imports BaseSettings from pydantic.
decision_rules.then: Add `pydantic-settings` to the project dependencies and update the import to `from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings`. Keep the change local to settings code first.

decision_rules.condition: The project intentionally requires Pydantic v1 compatibility because upstream dependencies are not v2-ready.
decision_rules.then: Pin or constrain Pydantic v1 only as an explicit compatibility decision, document the reason, and avoid mixing v1-only imports with v2-only dependency ranges.

decision_rules.condition: The import path is already pydantic_settings but the application still fails.
decision_rules.then: Do not keep applying this trap. Diagnose installation environment, missing pydantic-settings, settings validation, `.env` loading, or package resolver mismatch.

do_not: Do not blindly downgrade Pydantic to v1 as the first fix for a v2 project.
Do not change all Pydantic model code when only settings imports are failing.
